author: James Joyce
introFa: کتاب «A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man» نوشته James Joyce یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: evolution described by Sigmund Freud, for whom civilization had as much to do with biology as with behavior. As human beings stood erect, lifting their noses above the lower regions of the body, men be- gan to use sight rather than smell to choose their female sexual part- ners, Freud suggested. Cyclical mating gave way to more or less con- tinual mating, leading ultimately to “the founding of the family,” which Freud considered the hallmark of civilization (qtd. in Miller 71). “Standing up does more than reverse the value of menstrual odor,” writes William Miller, assessing Freud’s argument; “it paves the way for the devaluation of everything in the genital region,” including men- struation, human waste, and the smells of the erotic (72). “Olfaction, formerly the engine of desire, now founds the very capacity to be dis- gusted by those things once desired. So it comes to be that disgust keeps us on our feet and out of bed” (72-73). This process is enacted not only within the species but also within the individual, so that infants learn to revile bodily waste, to stigmatize “body odors, sexual or otherwise,” and to feel shame for the various protrusions, tubes, and openings that constitute the genital area (Drobnick 258-59). Only neurotics and hysterics, according to Freud, maintain a strong “pleasure” in waste or scent (Mavor 282). For them, waste and “particularly odorous” smells “recall the body of the mother and the coprophilic [having an interest in excrement] pleasure of a long lost childhood,” when they possessed “an unselfconscious attitude to- ward human waste” (Mavor 282; Cohen xviii). It is this cloacal past that Father Arnall invokes in his “noisome” hell, where the souls of those who have “defile[d] and pollute[d]” God and themselves are eternally subjected to feces, rotting flesh, “intolerable stench[es],” and “unbreathable . . . air” (Joyce 133, 131, 129). Foul matter, noxious smells, and “the evil seed of lust” are entangled in Arnall’s threatening exposition as, similarly, effluvia, scent, and sex are entangled in Freud’s theory of human evolution. The difference is that what Arnall sees as sin, Freud sees as psychological regression (113). The nineteenth-century “bourgeoisie ‘obsession’with filthiness and An Education in the Unwholesome 37

stink,” reflected in Portrait and manifest in its critics, has been widely documented (Cohen xxiv). As Miller notes, the “massive construction of underground sewers” that marked this century throughout Europe meant that city streets were no longer permeated by “the ubiquitous stench of feces and decaying animal matter” (78). Seeking to distin- guish themselves from their own noxious waste, among which they had so recently lived, Europeans identified public sewers as contaminative spaces. “The new Hell, the lower gastrointestinal base for the civilization resting upon it,” the sewer was seen as a site of pol- lution, both literally and symbolically (78). By the end of the century, not only had “stink” become an “improper” word to use in “polite con- versation,” but prominent sexologists such as Richard von Krafft-Ebing and Havelock Ellis were asserting that “a pronounced in- terest in odors” was a characteristic of “moral degenerat[es],” “‘primi- tives,’” and the mentally ill (Miller 78; Drobnick 257). According to these sexologists and other nineteenth-century “scientists,” these same groups displayed a heightened interest in sex. Further, these interests sometimes coincided—in the form of olfactophilia (sexual arousal caused by bodily smells) and osphresiophilia (sexual arousal caused by smells generally thought to be foul). The early accusations that Por- trait’s author displayed a “preoccupation with the olfactory,” could “never resist a dunghill,” probed subjects “which modern drainage [has] . . . taken out of ordinary intercourse,” and “would be really at his best in a treatise on drains” were undergirded by the belief that an inter- est in dirt, smell, and sex was a sign of moral filth (Squire 100; Wells 86; “Unsigned Review, Everyman” 85). Joyce’s moral character, in short, was in question. Sex, like dirt and stench, was considered inappropriate for “ordi- nary . . . conversation” (Wells 86), but like them it pervaded the nine- teenth-century consciousness. Overturning the long-standing belief that Victorians spoke little about and indulged less in sex, French phi- losopher Michel Foucault famously offers his repressive hypothesis in The History of Sexuality. Branding sex a taboo subject, he argues, actu- 38 Critical Insights

ally served as a “polymorphous incitement to discourse” (34). In other words, the social interdiction against sexual chatter generated more. Inciting the taboo in an attempt to manage attitudes toward sex, social institutions compelled individuals to internalize their interdicts, thereby, in essence, policing themselves. As a representative of the Church, Father Arnall, expounding at length on the forbidden, incul- cates such self-policing in his listeners. As belated Victorians, Joyce’s earliest critics, accusing the modernist author of “plung[ing] and drag[ging] his readers . . . into the slime of foul sewers,” enacted such self-policing (“Unsigned Review, Freeman’s” 98). In exposing the conflation of dirt, smell, and desire, I follow the practice of Janice Carlisle, author of Common Scents: Comparative Encounters in High-Victorian Fiction, for assessing smell in fiction. Like her, I read something as a smell, whether person, object, memory, or concept, only if it is “explicitly described as giving off a smell” in the text; “even obvious odorants like [farm animals] and sewers do not count if no one, character or narrator . . . , is depicted as noticing their exhalations” (5). I do not, in other words, assume stench simply be- cause there is filth. So while I would classify a sewer as an example of filth, I would not classify it as a smell unless the text expressly attrib- utes it with emitting one. Examples of desire in Portrait include mas- turbation and prostitution, whose representations are unambiguous; homosexuality, allusions to which, though once overlooked or glossed over briefly, have in more recent years been expatiated by prominent Joyceans; and fetishism (a component of Stephen’s attraction to both his mother and E. C.), remarked upon by Freudians old and new.2 As critics have long noted, “The opening section of the novel ren- ders a child’s sensuous and emotional response to stimuli,” including his own waste (Carens 271). But other than Stephen’s urine, dirt (or waste) figures only minimally in part 1. The most notable instantia- tions are the “cold slimy water” of the “square ditch” (an open cess- pool) into which Wells shoulders Stephen, “the dirty water” in the ho- tel sink, and the “warm turfcoloured bogwater” of the boys’bath, all of An Education in the Unwholesome 39

which recall Stephen’s urine-soaked bedclothes (Joyce 7, 8, 20). In each case, Stephen processes liquid filth through the sensation of touch, assessing it as warm, cold, or both in sequence. Smell is quickly established as a strong, if not “the strongest,” sensory “cue . . . for Ste- phen” (Valente, “Thrilled” 61), but it is not the primary means by which he interprets filth. Though he does ascribe a “queer smell” to the square’s “stale water,” as he did the clean oil sheet, Stephen finds only one smell unpleasant in part 1: altar wine, which makes him “feel a lit- tle sickish” because it reminds him of the “faint winy smell [of] the rec- tor’s breath” at his first communion (43, 47). Father Conmee’s study has “a strange solemn smell . . . like the old leather of chairs”; the char- coal burned by the acolyte has a “weak sour”—but not necessarily of- fensive—“smell”; and the medicine Stephen takes at the infirmary is “stinking stuff to drink,” though it is not attributed with any smell (58, 41, 20). The many expressly or connotatively good smells in part 1 include Stephen’s “sweet-smelling guardian,” as Suzette Henke (318) de- scribes Stephen’s mother, who “had a nicer smell than his father” (Joyce 3); the “lovely warm smell” of her slippers (7); “the warm heavy smell of turkey and ham and celery” at his “first Christmas din- ner” (28); the “cold night smell,” “a holy smell,” of the chapel at Clongowes (15); “the lovely smell . . . of Clane: rain and wintry air and turf smouldering and corduroy,” a smell shared by “its old peasants who knelt at the back of the chapel at Sunday mass” (17, 15); and “the smell of evening in the air, the smell of the fields in the country” (61). We can thus conclude that while young Stephen’s perception is partic- ularly olfactory, it is by no means occupied with the putrid; and while his memories of Clongowes are somewhat sodden, they are by no means foul. Stephen’s innocent desire to marry Eileen and his Oedipal attrac- tion to his mother are the principal examples of Stephen’s desire in part 1. Of these, smell figures affirmatively in his assessment of his mother and dirt not at all. The “smugging”—unspecified homosexual 40 Critical Insights

activity—of a few of Clongowes’s older boys is vaguely associated with the dirty square where they were rumored to have been caught, but this association is made by Stephen’s peers, who, unlike Stephen, have a clearer sense of the sexual nature of the purported crime (42). That the location of the smugging is as indeterminate as the smugging itself suggests not only the boys’ assumption that the wrongdoing in- volved sex but also that sex, at least when homosexual, is dirty. Filth figures moderately in part 2 of the novel, but it is not connected to stench. In Stephen’s estimation, the pubs he visits with his father and Uncle Charles on their Sunday constitutionals are “grimy,” but their odor goes unremarked (64). Stephen’s heart is “sickened” by the “sight of the filthy cowyard at Stradbrook with its foul green puddles and clots of dung and steaming brantroughs,” but it is the sight of the cows and not their smell that “revolted him” (66). Though the smells that scent the pages of part 2 may offend the average nose, they do not seem to trouble Stephen. From his point of olfaction, cigarette smoke gives off a “faint aromatic odour” while the “rank heavy air” of “horse piss and rotted straw” is to him a “good odour,” one that “calm[s] his heart” (79, 91). It may thus be that the “stale odours of the foreshore,” which Stephen and his gang frequent, do the same (91, 65). “Odour,” as we learn in the final evocative sentence of part 2, is for Stephen as “soft” and soothing as the “parting lips” of the prostitute to whom he “surrender[s]” (108). By part 2, Stephen has, however, begun to accept the association be- tween desire and moral filth, and between squalor and moral filth, that Father Arnall later articulates so forcefully. Stephen’s “mind and home,” the former increasingly lustful, the latter increasingly de- graded, feel to him “squalid” and “sordid” (83, 106). The word “fœtus,” which Stephen finds carved into a desk in a Cork “anatomy theatre,” reflects to him his own “monstrous reveries” (as he thinks of his sexual fantasies) and “mad and filthy orgies” (as he thinks of his masturbatory activities), reminding him of the “squalor of his life and . . . the riot of his mind” (95, 96-97, 96). As Joseph Valente and An Education in the Unwholesome 41

Margot Backus have suggested, this is a somewhat incongruous re- sponse to “medical graffiti” (538). But for Stephen, who is learning to read the body as dirty, this mark of vandalism, a mark connected in its own way to sex, easily recalls his own “defile[ment],” both of his body and of those that figure in his onanistic fantasies (Joyce 105). In con- trast to “the vigour of rude male health” possessed by implicitly nor- mal young men, Stephen sees his own physical state as abject: “his blood . . . in revolt,” “his hands clenched convulsively and his teeth set together as he suffered the agony of . . . penetration” by “some dark presence moving irresistibly upon him” (102, 106). No longer “capa- ble of simple joys,” he is consumed by “the wasting fires of lust,” choked by “the cry . . . in his throat,” “a cry which was but the echo of an obscene scrawl which he had read on the oozing wall of a urinal” (102, 106). Where once Stephen associated the body and its senses with pleasure, he has come to see them as a source of shame. Where once he accepted his desire for the “nice”-smelling maternal body, he has come to see himself as a “prowling beast,” “wandering up and down the dark slimy street[s] and peering into the gloom of lanes and doorways,” in search of the “maternal arms” of a “perfumed” “doll” (Joyce 3, 106; Brivic 287; Joyce 107). The infant lying contentedly in his own urine has become the adolescent reading his own desires in the “obscene” signposting of fecal smear (106). The familiar has become the foul, as desire, like waste, has been polluted by shame. The sermons that constitute the majority of part 3 “reproduce mi- metically in the reader what Stephen himself is undergoing”: the pres- sure of indoctrination against “sensual impulses” (Wollaeger 17; Mahaffey 208). As fetid as they are fiery, as abject as they are artful, Father Arnall’s sermons depict a putrid, pungent eternity that awaits the unrepentant sinner. This malignant hell is filled with rotting corpses, “human fungus,” “fumes of nauseous loathsome decomposi- tion,” “suffocating filth,” “offal,” and “scum” (Joyce 130, 129, 131, 129). Its smells are “sickening,” “horrible” (130), “awful,” “pestilen- tial,” “reeking,” “intolerable,” and “unbreathable (129). In this dirty 42 Critical Insights

and “foulsmelling prison,” the “defile[d] and pollute[d]” soul, “tor- tured” by the “noisome odours” of filth, “loathe[s]” itself for “the im- pure and adulterous and unspeakable and filthy pleasures in which [it] delighted” (128, 133, 131, 139). As Arnall sees it, it is an apt punish- ment for the soul that has “consent[ed] to the promptings of . . . the lower instincts, to that which is gross” (131, 137). Even before the retreat, the “doctrines of the church” have con- vinced Stephen that his unconfessed “lust” ensures his “condemna- tion,” though he is unwilling to do anything about it (113). Stephen’s sense of his own degradation steadily intensifies as he listens to Arnall, until at last he confesses, “his sins trickl[ing] from his lips, one by one, trickl[ing] in shameful drops from his soul, festering and oozing like a sore, a squalid stream of vice[,] . . . sluggish [and] filthy” (156). Listen- ing to the preacher, he imagines “his soul fattening and congealing into a gross grease,” his “sweat oozing upon his skin,” his body dying, then, becoming a corpse, “thrust . . . out of sight into a long hole in the ground into the grave, to rot, to feed the mass of its creeping worms and to be devoured by scuttling plumpbellied rats” (120). While the thrust, the hole, the worms, and the swollen bellies suggest the sexual nature of his sin, the grease, the sweat, the corpse, the rot, and the rats reflect its filth. Convinced that “every word” of the sermon “was for him,” “he felt now that his soul was festering in sin”; “like a beast in its lair,” it was lying “down in its own filth” (123). “Foul memories con- densed within his brain,” “shame covered him wholly like fine glow- ing ashes,” and “his soul sickened at the thought of a torpid snaky life feeding itself out of the tender marrow of his life and fattening upon the slime of lust” (124, 154, 151). Throughout part 3, the guilt Stephen feels over his sexual sins is conveyed through the language of filth. During the course of the retreat Stephen comes to associate his sexual impulses with stench, so that “the sordid details of his orgies stank un- der his very nostrils” (124). By the end of the retreat, he sees and smells himself as “utterly abject[]” (136). The evening before his confession, Stephen, employing Arnall’s An Education in the Unwholesome 43

conflationary logic, reflects on the particulars of sexual sins that he en- acted “secretly, filthily, time after time” (148). Hiding his face beneath his hands, he envisions a field of fiendish “creatures,” surrounded by “clots and coils of solid excrement” from which “an evil smell, faint and foul as the light, curled upwards” (148). The creatures moved in slow circles, circling closer and closer to enclose, to enclose, soft language issuing from their lips, their long swishing tails besmeared with stale shite, thrusting upwards their terrific faces. . . . . . . That was his hell. God had allowed him to see the hell reserved for his sins: stinking, bestial, malignant, a hell of lecherous goatish fiends. For him! For him! He sprang from the bed, the reeking odour pouring down his throat, clogging and revolting his entrails. Air! The air of heaven! He stumbled to- wards the window, groaning and almost fainting with sickness. At the washstand a convulsion seized him within; and, clasping his cold forehead wildly, he vomited profusely in agony. (149) “Lecherous” creatures with “thrusting” faces and “shite”-besmirched tails engulf the conscience-ridden Stephen (148). “The reeking odour” of his guilty nightmare enters his nose, descends his throat and blocks his entrails. In revolt, his body expels the stench, with all its sinful as- sociations, back up through his throat and out the mouth “whereon [once] lingered foul and shameful words, the savor . . . of a lewd kiss” (112). Arnall’s sermons, exemplary instantiations of the indoctrination to which Stephen has long been subjected, have produced in the six- teen-year-old not just a “frenzy to confess” but also, more extensively, a submission to the values of his Jesuit education—repugnance, in other words, for the filthy and the fetid, and the belief that most forms of sex are both (Castle 165). In the “fragrant shadow of the church,” Stephen confesses until he has nothing left to say, after which he imag- ines “his prayers ascend[ing] to heaven from his purified heart like per- fume streaming upwards from the heart of a white rose” (Joyce 157). 44 Critical Insights

“His soul,” which such a short time before was “foul with sin,” has be- come as “fragrant” as the “masses of white flowers” “heaped” on the altar at which he now kneels (153, 158). Filth all but disappears in the novel’s penultimate chapter, in which Stephen atones for his sins. Submitting himself to milder versions of the sensory punishments of Father Arnall’s hell, Stephen undertakes a series of “mortifications,” bringing “each of his senses . . . under a rigorous discipline” (162). “His sense of smell,” however, is “re- volted” by “only one odor”: “a certain stale fishy stink like that of long-standing urine,” to which “he subjected himself” whenever he could (163). Though Stephen has come to associate sex with sin and sin with stench, he has not gone so far as to associate olfaction itself with the sexual, the excremental, or the fetid. In fact, “he found in him- self no instinctive repugnance to bad odours whether they were the odours of the outdoor world, such as those of dung or tar, or the odours of his own person among which he had made many curious compari- sons and experiments” (163). Despite this relative immunity to stench, Stephen has learned to assign positive value to a lack of scent, as evinced by his sense that “the rosaries which he said constantly . . . transformed themselves into” “odourless” “coronals of flowers” (160). By way of contrast, “the names of articles of dress worn by women or of certain soft and delicate stuffs used in their making brought always to his mind a delicate and sinful perfume” (168). The connection be- tween stench and desire that Stephen made on the retreat may not linger, but the belief that desire is sinful persists. Following the retreat, Stephen abstains from sex, with himself and others, though he ultimately rejects the “passionless life” of the priest- hood (174). As he attempts to imagine what his experience as a novi- tiate would be like, he recalls “the troubling odour of the long corridors of Clongowes” and “smelt again the warm moist air which hung in [its] bath above the sluggish turfcoloured water” (174). These smells, the latter ambivalent, the former indeterminate, are for Stephen associated with “the chill and order” of institutional Jesuit life (174). Returning An Education in the Unwholesome 45

home after declining the director’s invitation to join the priesthood, Stephen smells “the faint sour stink of rotted cabbages . . . from the kitchen gardens on the rising ground above the river. He smiled to think that it was this disorder, the misrule and confusion of his father’s house and the stagnation of vegetable life, which was to win the day in his soul” (176). Rejecting a logic that carves the world into halves, rank and odorless, dirty and clean, sinner and saved, Stephen has be- gun to accept the fact that rot, stench, and imperfection are natural parts of life. By the end of the novel, Stephen has discarded the belief that dirt is foul. Walking through Dublin’s streets at the start of part 5, “he was glad to find himself still in the midst of common lives, passing on his way amid the squalor . . . of the city fearlessly and with a light heart” (191). He even allows for the possibility that something as quintessentially filthy and abject as excrement could be art. “If not why not?” he provocatively asks his friend Lynch (232). As altar wine was the only smell that offended Stephen in part 1, so in part 5 only one smell “assailed him”: the “cheerless cellardamp and decay” permeat- ing University College, both in the classroom and in the gardens out- side (192). Refusing to “serve that in which [he] no longer believe[s],” Stephen has rejected the church he sees as “the scullerymaid of chris- tendom” (228, 239), associating it, not his desires, with dank smells and “dirty work” (“Scullery”). He has also begun to relearn sensuous pleasure. “He allowed his mother to scrub his neck and root into the folds of his ears and into the interstices at the wings of his nose,” to reach into his cavities and tease out their dirt (Joyce 189). Walking through Dublin, he thinks of “girls and women,” characters in plays, without shame, their “memories . . . and the fragrance falling from the wet branches mingl[ing] in a mood of quiet joy” (190). Though he declines to pursue the elusive E. C., Ste- phen accepts his desire for her. 46 Critical Insights

He knew vaguely that her figure was passing homeward through the city. Vaguely first and then more sharply he smelt her body. A conscious unrest seethed in his blood. Yes, it was her body he smelt, a wild and languid smell, the tepid limbs over which his music had flowed desirously and the secret soft linen upon which her flesh distilled odour and a dew. (253-54) Stephen reads E. C.—even locates her—through her scent. Wild and warm, wet and fleshy, it is a scent composed of sexual notes that do not constitute the “sinful” bouquet he once associated with a woman’s body (168). While the object of Stephen’s desire remains scented, it has lost its aroma of shame. Stephen feels the “glow of [his] desire kindl[ing] . . . his soul and . . . fulfill[ing] all his body” as, preparing to write his villanelle, he thinks of E. C., “waking from odorous sleep,” “yield[ing]” “her nakedness . . . to him, radiant, warm, odorous and lavishlimbed, . . . enfold[ing] him like water with a liquid life” (242). An ambiguous word, sometimes denoting the fair scented, sometimes the foul scented, “odorous” is the perfect word, at once recalling Ste- phen’s earlier ascription of stench to desire and conveying the present aromatic associations desire holds for him. According to the directors of Stephen’s religious education, dirt, odor, and desire are pollutants that threaten both body and soul. As Joyce suggests in the sensuous opening of the novel, however, the child delights in all three. Taught to revile these consistently conflated elements, Stephen undergoes a journey into shame and back out again. Learning, adopting, then unlearning the attitudes toward dirt, stench, and desire so passionately detailed by Father Arnall at the pungent heart of the novel, Stephen traverses the psychological minefield of his Jesuit education. He does not, however, escape unscathed, for his un- willingness to pursue the girl for whom he so clearly longs, like his un- willingness to bathe shortly after the death of his mother (noted in Ulysses), reflects, while not the shame of desire, its unwholesome residue. The Smithy of Stephen Dedalus’s Soul in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man: Contexts for Joyce’s Novel Maureen O’Connor Late in James Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, the protagonist, Stephen Dedalus, at this point a student at University Col- lege Dublin (UCD), asserts his intellectual singularity, expressing in his own words the “slow and dark birth” of his soul. He declares: “When the soul of a man is born in this country there are nets flung at it to hold it back from flight. You talk to me of nationality, language, reli- gion. I shall try to fly by those nets.” This assertion signals Stephen’s independence, his putting away of childish things, in the words of Saint Paul. This is the final development toward which the bildungs- roman has been working. To appreciate just how startlingly defiant and iconoclastic such a statement would have been, both to Stephen’s inter- locutors and to Joyce’s early readers, it is necessary to understand the nature of these “nets,” which the author himself never entirely evaded, entanglements evident in the life of the novel’s protagonist from his earliest perceptions, from baby Stephen’s lisping evocation of “the little green place” on the novel’s very first page. Nationality Joyce’s novel is set in the last decades of the nineteenth century and the first years of the twentieth century, a time when what was referred to as the “Irish Question,” that is, the question of Irish nationalism, specifically in terms of the relationship between England and Ireland, was growing in intensity. It often erupted in violence and bloodshed. From the twelfth century, when the Normans landed in Ireland and King Henry II of England invaded with the blessing of Pope Adrian IV, the English Crown had struggled to subdue the “natives” and to rule the island, a rule periodically resisted in a series of unsuccessful rebel- 50 Critical Insights

lions over the centuries. The last of these, the Easter Rising of 1916, which set in motion the events leading to Ireland’s ultimate indepen- dence, had not yet taken place when Joyce was writing Portrait, but the need for such an action was being urgently debated and even ac- tively prepared for by some of its key figures, including one of its lead- ers and subsequent martyrs, Patrick Pearse, who gave Joyce lessons in the Irish language. Two significant figures in the history of Ireland’s nationalist struggle are present throughout the novel: Theobald Wolfe Tone and Charles Stewart Parnell, the latter appearing as early as the opening impressionistic scenes of Stephen’s first memories. In a public lecture, “Ireland, Island of Saints and Sages,” delivered in Trieste in 1907, Joyce makes clear his regard for what he calls the “heroes” of the 1798 rebellion, including “Lord Edward Fitzgerald, Robert Emmet, Theobald Wolfe Tone, and Napper Tandy.” He saves his greatest praise for “Charles Stewart Parnell, who was perhaps the most formidable man that ever led the Irish” (Joyce 162). The modern Irish nationalist movement could be said to have begun with Tone’s founding of the Society of United Irishmen. Its aim was to secure ex- tended rights for the Irish and independence for their country. Initially the United Irishmen campaigned for parliamentary reform, but the so- ciety evolved into a revolutionary separatist movement that culmi- nated in armed rebellion in 1798. The uprising, inspired by the French and American revolutions, and to some extent supported by French forces, was undone by a number of factors, including informers to the Crown. English forces reacted violently, with wide-scale massacres. The uprising led to the Act of Union in 1801, which created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, securing London’s centrality in determining Irish affairs. The Irish Parliament, which beginning in the 1780s had achieved some measure of legislative independence, was dissolved. Daniel O’Connell, known as “the Liberator” (by which name Stephen mentions him in his early days at Clongowes Wood Col- lege, a pricey Jesuit school for boys where he is trying to determine his standing among the other status-conscious pupils), established the Re- Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 51

peal Association in 1840, which agitated for repeal of the union to England. The cause was pursued in different forms and under different banners throughout the century and after. Stephen’s nationalist father reveres the memory of Tone, at whose memorial plaque in Dublin Stephen recalls him laying a wreath: Ste- phen “remembered with bitterness that scene of tawdry tribute,” at- tended by only a few French delegates and a young man holding a stick with a sign reading “Vive l’Irlande.” This is one of the many moments of Stephen’s ambivalence toward the national cause. He is “bitter” about the lack of recognition of a hero of that cause, even though a few pages later he treats with sneering disdain the fervent nationalism of his friend Davin, whom he calls a “young fenian,” mawkishly wor- shipping “the sorrowful legend of Ireland.” Fenianism was the violent republican movement against British rule in the latter half of the nine- teenth century. It began in the United States with the Fenian Brother- hood, initially a coalition of emigrants who had fled the Great Famine of 1845-52, a cataclysm responsible for reducing the Irish population by over a million through starvation, eviction, disease, and emigration. In contrast to the condemnation implicit in Stephen’s identification of Davin with Fenian extremism, Joyce, in his 1907 “Saints and Sages” talk, credits “Fenian violence” with the revocation of the penal laws that had greatly restricted the rights of Irish Roman Catholics (168). Stephen makes a joke of Davin’s passions by calling him one of the “tame geese,” a reference to the “Wild Geese,” Irish soldiers who fled the country at the disastrous conclusion of the Williamite War of 1691, the first serious exodus of the Irish from their native country (a prece- dent for the waves of mass leave-taking that were to continue through the late twentieth century). This oscillation between genuine engage- ment with the question of nation and flippant derogation, Stephen’s and Joyce’s shifting evaluation of heroic republicanism, reflects not only the author’s own mixed feelings but also those of many Irishmen. They were divided in their loyalties to competing versions of Irish pa- triotism, as exemplified in the polarized reactions to the fall of Parnell, 52 Critical Insights

“the Chief,” the “uncrowned king of Ireland,” as both Stephen’s and Joyce’s fathers (and many of their contemporaries) referred to their fallen leader. The novel’s first mention of Parnell occurs at the beginning of the narrative, when young Stephen recalls brushes belonging to his aunt “Dante”: “The brush with the maroon velvet back was for Michael Davitt and the brush with the green velvet back was for Parnell.” Mi- chael Davitt was a member of the Irish Revolutionary Brotherhood (IRB) who spent time in jail for smuggling arms into Ireland and who in 1879 founded the Land League, an organization devoted to the rights of tenant farmers and the reformation of exploitative policies re- garding the ownership of land. Davitt brought Parnell, then Home Rule Party member of Parliament, into the Land League as its leader. In his role as president of the league, though an Irish Protestant landlord him- self, Parnell exerted considerable influence on land reform legislation and the direction of the Land Wars, fought over the restoration to the Roman Catholic “native” Irish of land lost to British Protestant settlers over the centuries. As chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party, Parnell came close to securing the passage of a Home Rule Bill in 1886, a proposed law intended to grant Ireland legislative indepen- dence within the union, for which he won support from Prime Minister William Gladstone. One of Parnell’s most significant accomplishments was the unifica- tion of the many strands of Irish nationalism, a short-lived success be- cause the party split in 1890 when Parnell was named in a divorce peti- tion that revealed his decade-long affair that produced three children with Katherine O’Shea, the wife of one of his parliamentary col- leagues. Enemies called her “Kitty,” a term used for prostitutes. The Catholic Church denounced the “adulterer.” Davitt himself demanded Parnell’s resignation. This scandal drives the pious Dante to tear the green backing off her brush, leaving young Stephen to wonder whether Parnell is “a bad man.” Parnell refused to step down despite the de- struction of his reputation and political power; he married Katherine in Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 53

1891, but died soon after. In Portrait, Joyce has Parnell’s death coin- cide with Stephen’s stay in the Clongowes Wood College infirmary be- cause he is sick after having been shoved into the square ditch, an ex- posed cesspool. Stephen feels sorry for himself and experiences the announcement of the momentous event as part of a waking fever dream. The excessive romanticizing of the death in confused, childish visions suggests some irony regarding the elevation of the “uncrowned king,” yet Joyce’s own obsession with the figure of Parnell, with whose persecution the sometimes paranoid writer identified, is well documented. Parnell provided the subject of “Et Tu, Healy” (Ellmann 33), Joyce’s now lost first poem, written when he was nine; of “Ivy Day in the Committee Room,” one of the stories in Joyce’s collection Dubliners; and of the poem “Gas from a Burner.” Joyce often wrote and spoke about the fallen leader’s fascinating personality, as in his 1912 essay “The Shade of Parnell.” Some of Joyce’s difficulties with the kind of Irish nationalism de- veloping around him, as the old century gave way to the new, related to to his own artistic struggles in a country casting about for a non- English identity, not only in matters of land reform and political inde- pendence but also at the level of culture. Earlier in the nineteenth cen- tury, “cultural nationalism” distinguished the work of Young Ireland, a movement that grew out of O’Connell’s repeal agitation. This group of intellectuals founded a newspaper, The Nation, first printed in 1842 and dedicated to the spirit of 1798. The publication was suppressed by the British in 1848 after the failed Young Irelander Rebellion. The newspaper featured journalism and poetry by writers such as James Clarence Mangan (a poet of great importance to Joyce), John Kells Ingram, and Thomas Davis. As the Irish emerged from the worst of the midcentury famine’s devastation, renewed interest in reestablishing a uniquely Irish culture led to the turn-of-the-century Irish Literary Re- vival, featuring most famously the poet William Butler Yeats, whom the young Joyce made several attempts to impress. In 1882, Yeats, along with Standish James O’Grady, the Fenian John O’Leary, and 54 Critical Insights

Douglas Hyde, founded the Irish National Literary Society, a body dedicated to the study and dissemination of Irish literature and folk- lore. In a famous address to the society in 1892, “The Necessity for De-Anglicizing Ireland,” Hyde observed that “the Irish race is at pres- ent in a most anomalous position, imitating England and yet apparently hating it” (3), a sentiment with which Joyce would agree. Hyde went on to call for the Irishman to set his face against this constant running to England for our books, litera- ture, music, games, fashions, and ideas. I appeal to every one whatever his politics—for this is no political matter—to do his best to help the Irish race to develop in future upon Irish lines, even at the risk of encouraging na- tional aspirations. (11) According to Joyce biographer Richard Ellmann, Hyde, O’Grady, O’Leary, and Yeats “made Dublin an intellectual center, and in spite of his careful dissociation of himself from many shibboleths of the new literature, Joyce profited from its momentum” (98). Joyce, Ellmann tells us, was prepared to meet “demands of his country for national feeling” but “detested the grosser forms of nationalism” (66). One of the “grosser forms” of Irish nationality to which Joyce objected was language revival, the very tool Hyde identified as the most powerful in the project of de-Anglicizing. Language It was not “The Necessity for De-Anglicizing Ireland” but another production of Hyde’s that led to Joyce’s decisive disenchantment with Irish cultural nationalism and the Literary Revival envisioned by Yeats. In Portrait, we see Stephen remembering “the night of the open- ing of the national theatre.” The scene that follows is a version of the threat of disturbance and consequent police attendance at the opening night of the 1899 performance of Yeats’s The Countess Cathleen, Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 55

which Joyce attended when still a student at UCD. The play was pro- duced by the Irish Literary Theatre, founded by Yeats, Edward Martyn, and Lady Gregory among others, which led to creation of the Irish Na- tional Theatre, ultimately named the Abbey Theatre. Joyce did not sympathize with his fellow students’ vehement objections to The Countess Cathleen’s representation of the peasantry. At this point he supported Yeats’s vision, eagerly seeking the poet’s patronage and ap- proval through the intercession of George Russell, also known as Æ. Joyce recommended the inclusion in the theater’s repertoire of works from other European nations that Joyce would translate. Despite vague encouragement from Yeats, Joyce was disgusted to discover that the theater was instead becoming hopelessly parochial, emphasizing texts drawn from Irish folktales, myths, and legends, including plays in Irish, beginning with Douglas Hyde’s Casadh-an-tSúgáin (The Twist- ing of the Rope). Hyde’s play was staged in October 1901, and Joyce immediately de- nounced the direction Yeats’s theater was taking in an excoriating arti- cle, “The Day of the Rabblement.” He could find no one to willing to publish it, however, so he and his fellow student Francis Skeffington, who was having trouble placing an article of his own on the issue of equal access to education for women, published their articles together as a leaflet that they distributed around Dublin. In “The Day of the Rabblement,” Joyce declared that the Irish Literary Theatre was not the “champion of progress” it claimed to be, but had allowed the “popular devil” to prevail: The Irish Literary Theatre must now be considered the property of the rabblement of the most belated race in Europe. A nation which never ad- vanced so far as a miracle-play affords no literary model to the artist, and he must look abroad. (70) A few years later, in his “Saints and Sages” lecture, Joyce would make a similar point: 56 Critical Insights

Even a superficial consideration will show us that the Irish nation’s insis- tence on developing its own culture by itself is not so much the demand of a young nation that wants to make good in the European concert as the de- mand of a very old nation to renew itself under new forms the glories of a past civilization. (157) Joyce’s—and Stephen’s—reservations about the nation often con- cerned language and the dwelling on Ireland’s troubled past. Hyde’s nationalist credentials included founding in 1893, with Eoin MacNeill, the Gaelic League (Connradh na Gaeilge), an organization committed to promoting Irish as a spoken language and to the preser- vation of all aspects of “Gaelic” culture, including dance, music, and traditional Irish industries. By the end of the nineteenth century, the Irish language was in danger of extinction. As Joyce himself observed in his 1907 “Saints and Sages” lecture, “Ten years ago [Irish] was spo- ken only by the peasants in the western provinces on the coast of the Atlantic and a few in the south, and on the little islands that stand like pickets on the vanguard of Europe, on the front of the eastern hemi- sphere” (155). The popular theory was, and continues to be, that the famine wiped out most native speakers. However, the decline of the language began before the famine, as early as 1829, with Catholic Emancipation, which allowed the Roman Catholic population to gain access to education, to enter the professions, and to worship freely. No longer were the native Irish restricted to the peasantry. With mid- dle-class status came concerns about propriety and “high” culture, the available model being English. Speaking Irish was associated with shameful, downtrodden peasants, a rustic, rural identity that Stephen’s urban and urbane father, an inveterate Dubliner, refers to as “Paddy Stink and Mickey Mud.” This lingering fear of inferiority, a conflicted resentment toward all things English, even as they represent all desirable attainments, contin- ues paradoxically to distinguish the Irish experience. One of the most frequently quoted passages in Portrait is the conversation between Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 57

Stephen and the university’s English dean of studies, in the course of which Stephen refers to a “tundish,” a dialectal word for funnel that the dean does not know. Stephen interprets the dean’s professed interest in the unusual word as condescending. His response is typically defiant: The language in which we are speaking is his before it is mine. How differ- ent are the words home, Christ, ale, master, on his lips and on mine! I can- not speak or write these words without unrest of spirit. His language, so fa- miliar and so foreign, will always be for me an acquired speech. I have not made or accepted its words. My voice holds them at bay. My soul frets in the shadow of his language. Stephen’s statement is worth considering in light of Joyce’s reasons for abandoning his own early attempts at Irish lessons: he strenuously objected to Pearse’s insistence that Irish is superior to English, which Pearse regularly mocked as verbally “inadequate” (Ellmann 61). Ironi- cally, Irish was one of the few European languages Joyce did not have much knowledge of until late in his life. In Portrait, while arguing about nationalism, Stephen’s friend Davin calls him a “born sneerer.” Stephen’s rejoinder is to associate nationalism with the “indispensible informer,” a reference to the betrayals of Tone and Parnell. In this ex- change we learn that Stephen, like Joyce, “drop[ped] out of the [Gaelic] league class after the first lesson.” Stephen defends this by disparaging his ancestors who “threw off their own language” and “al- lowed a handful of foreigners to subject them.” He sees no reason to pay off their debt. When Davin argues that he should do so “for our freedom,” Stephen asserts, “No honorable and sincere man . . . has given up to you his life and his youth and his affections from the days of Tone to those of Parnell but you sold him to the enemy or failed him in need or reviled him and left him for another.” One ostensible irony here is that Stephen’s resolute resistance to nationalism is enabled by his identification with two of its heroes; the more disabling irony, how- ever, is that he has quit his Irish lessons not out of lofty convictions but 58 Critical Insights

out of petty jealousy over what he believes is a flirtation between a young woman he admires and the priest who is giving the lessons. We see similar ambivalence in the treatment of the Irish language in the best known of Joyce’s short stories, “The Dead.” At the party that opens the story, the protagonist, Gabriel Conroy, is twitted by the na- tionalist Miss Ivors for not knowing his own country, for holidaying on the Continent instead of in Ireland. He protests that such travel helps him “keep in touch with the languages,” to which Miss Ivors replies, “And haven’t you your own language to keep in touch with—Irish?” Gabriel insists that Irish is not his language. This assertion of the so- phisticated superiority of the continental over the parochial must be re- considered by the story’s end when Gabriel is revealed to be so self- involved and blind to life as to know nothing about his wife, Gretta, to whom he has been married for many years and who is herself a countrywoman from the remote west of Ireland. The character embodying rustic “nationality” in Portrait is Davin, “the peasant student,” possibly named for Maurice Davin, the first president of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), which was founded in 1884 by “Michael Cusack, the Gael,” as he is called in Por- trait’s last chapter, in order to preserve and cultivate traditional sports and activities. Davin is repeatedly represented as holding a camán, or hurley, the stick used in hurling, an ancient Gaelic sport revived by the GAA. This passage leads to Stephen’s final gestures of self-formation, his “intellectual revolt” conducted largely through defiance of every- thing “traditional” and, therefore, to him, stifling. Much of his revolt consists of a rejection of all that his friend Davin stands for, including Irish: “His nurse had taught him Irish and shaped his rude imagination by the broken lights of Irish myth,” the lights that Joyce was convinced Yeats had mistakenly followed in the Literary Theatre. As with nation- ality, however, Joyce, and Stephen, relates to the issue of language in a tormented and sometimes contradictory way. Only a few lines after the condescending reference to Davin’s “rude imagination” and “Irish myth,” an observation is made regarding Stephen’s state of mind that Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 59

recalls Hyde’s “The Necessity for De-Anglicizing Ireland”: “Whatso- ever of thought or of feeling came to him from England or by way of English culture his mind stood armed against in obedience to a password.” Religion “The Irish, doomed to express themselves in a language that is not their own, have stamped it with their genius and compete for glory with other civilized countries. This,” according to Joyce, “is called ‘English Literature’” (qtd. in Bruni 28). The idea that English is not his native tongue recurs in Joyce’s writing, as does the conviction that it is never- theless English in which his “genius” glories. “If the Irish programme did not insist on the Irish language I suppose I could call myself a nation- alist” (qtd. in Ellmann 237), Joyce reveals in a letter to his brother Stanislaus in 1906. He is writing here about Arthur Griffith, chief archi- tect of the separatist political party founded in 1905, Sinn Féin (“Our- selves Alone,” or “We Ourselves,” as Joyce more accurately translates it). Joyce was, perhaps surprisingly, an advocate for Griffith and the goals of Sinn Féin, believing, as he told Stanislaus, that Griffith’s news- paper, United Irishman, “was the only one of any merit in Ireland.” He goes on to observe approvingly that Griffith “was the first person in Ire- land to revive the separatist idea on modern lines nine years ago” (qtd. in Ellmann 237). Ellmann credits Joyce’s interest in socialism as informing his admiration for Griffith and his anticapitalist, more specifically anti-English-capitalist, approach to the question of the nation. Also of significance for Joyce is that Griffith is an enemy of the priests: He is holding out some secular liberty to the people and the Church doesn’t approve of that. I quite see, of course, that the Church is still, as it was in the time of Adrian IV, the enemy of Ireland, but I think her time is almost up. For either Sinn Féin or Imperialism will conquer the present Ireland. (qtd. in Ellmann 237) 60 Critical Insights

According to Roy Foster, however, Griffith’s championing of the “Hun- garian model” of boycotting England can be seen as an endorsement of “his contemporaries among nationalist ideologues [who] defined ‘Irish’ in a way that implied, or even stated, its congruence with ‘Gaelic’ and ‘Catholic’” (13). Such a congruence would be anathema to Joyce, who declaimed against the foolishness of denying Irishness to anyone who might be “the descendent of a Cromwellian settler” (that is, Protestant); to do so would be “to deny it to almost all the heroes of the Irish move- ment,” including Tone and Parnell (Joyce 161-62). In the last pages of Portrait, Stephen’s friend Cranly fears that Ste- phen may convert to Protestantism. Stephen dismisses the idea: “I said that I had lost the faith, . . . not that I had lost self-respect. What kind of liberation would that be to forsake an absurdity which is logical and co- herent and to embrace one which is illogical and incoherent?” Despite Joyce’s atheism, his emotional and even intellectual fidelity to the Roman Catholic Church endured throughout his life. His aesthetic theory and practice were indebted to Catholic ritual and dogma, and he attended Mass as an observer wherever he lived in Europe. According to Edna O’Brien, he went so far as to prefer “blackberry jam because Christ’s crown of thorns came from that wood and he wore purple cra- vats during Lent” (13). Joyce found “a Protestant Ireland . . . almost unthinkable” (Joyce 169); indeed, Irish Catholicism can be understood as a constitutive part of the country’s rebellious identity. One of Ireland’s differences from the rest of what would become the United Kingdom lay in its obdurate resistance to the Protestant Refor- mation of the sixteenth century, which served to abet an increasingly “racialized” difference between the Irish and the English by the time of the famine. Unlike Wales, Scotland, and England, in Ireland the popu- lation remained largely Roman Catholic, even in the face of the seven- teenth-century Penal Laws against Catholics (also called “popery laws” and referred to by Cranly just before the exchange quoted Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 61

above). These laws forbade Catholics to worship (as the clergy was banned) and also restricted their access to education, property owner- ship, holding of public office, and the right to vote. By the late eigh- teenth century most of these restrictions had been lifted, perhaps most significantly for Portrait the banning of the clergy, as much of the nar- rative takes place in educational institutions run by priests. St. Pat- rick’s College in Maynooth was established in 1795, and priests were once more trained on Irish soil. With the Roman Catholic Relief Act in 1829, Catholic Emancipation (one of Daniel O’Connell’s campaigns, which he began to pursue in 1805) was granted, and most remaining restrictions were lifted, though the peasantry continued to be disenfranchised and denied rights to their land. Even before Emancipation, though still suppressed in Ireland, the Jesuits, members of the militantly Catholic Society of Jesus, created by its first “general,” Saint Ignatius Loyola, returned. Loyola sent the so- ciety’s first priests to Ireland in 1542, two years after the order’s con- firmation by the official church. Banished since the seventeenth cen- tury, they were led in their 1814 return by Father Peter Kenny, who immediately moved to open a school at Clongowes. The Jesuits were eventually a significant presence on the faculty of the Catholic Univer- sity of Ireland, founded in 1854 (which would become UCD in 1880). Most of Joyce’s teachers were Jesuits, though he also briefly attended a school run by the Christian Brothers. The Jesuits, the most respected teaching order, ran a number of elite schools, including those that, like Joyce, Stephen attends in Portrait, Clongowes Wood College in Kildare and Belvedere College, Dublin. The famous hellfire sermon that terrifies Stephen in chapter 3 of Portrait draws heavily on Ignatius Loyola’s Spiritual Exercises. Once again, in examining Joyce’s attitude toward the Jesuits, we find contradictions. To the end of his life he praised the education that the Jesuits provided and went so far as to instruct a friend writing about him to describe him not as a Catholic but “as a Jesuit” (qtd. in Ellmann 27). And yet, according to O’Brien, he referred to the Jesuits as a 62 Critical Insights

“heartless order that bears the name of Jesus by antiphrasis” (5). De- scribing the desolation of modern Ireland after centuries of the British government “having it by the throat,” he evokes a “briar patch. They sowed it with famine, syphilis, superstition and alcoholism. Up sprouted Puritans, Jesuits, and bigots” (qtd. in Bruni 27). Negative ste- reotypes about the Jesuits—that they were cunning and scheming, equivocating, evasive and untruthful—were also applied to the Irish (though the Jesuits were assumed to be operating at a higher, more “subtle” level). “Jesuitry” was a common synonym for casuistry, the misleading use of logic to settle ethical questions unethically. Both the negative and the positive associations with the order could be appeal- ing to an author who has Stephen Dedalus identify the weapons to be used in his struggle for freedom as “silence, exile, and cunning.” Joyce manifests similar attitudes toward the Catholic Church: ap- preciation and loyalty paradoxically coexisting with devastating cri- tique and passionate rejection. The Church is often a villain in Joyce’s ruminations on the evils that have beset Ireland. In his “Saints and Sages” lecture he equates the church with the sins of English rule: The soul of the country is weakened by centuries of useless struggle and bro- ken treaties, and individual initiative is paralyzed by the influence and admo- nitions of the church, while its body is manacled by the police, the tax office, and the garrison. No one who has any self-respect stays in Ireland. (171) Joyce names “Roman tyranny” (the tyranny of the Roman Catholic Church), which “occupies the place of the soul,” as something to be overthrown before “English tyranny” can be addressed (171). In a 1910 article titled “The Home Rule Comet,” Joyce implicitly charges Ireland’s slavish devotion with being the source of its shameful history of betraying patriots, the worst possible offense for Joyce: Ireland “has only served one master well, the Roman Catholic Church” (213). However, as already mentioned, the Church provided Joyce with a rich source of inspiration, both aesthetically and intellectually, and, like Contexts for Joyce’s Novel 63

Stephen, he did not turn away from it entirely. Stephen rejects conver- sion, but a hero of his in Portrait is the famous convert John Henry Newman, the first rector (president) of UCD. Newman left the Angli- can Church and in 1845 joined the Roman Catholic clergy. After leav- ing England for Ireland to help set up the Catholic University as an alternative to both Trinity College, which was not welcoming to Cath- olics, and the recently established nondenominational Queen’s Col- leges, Newman delivered a series of lectures in Dublin on Catholic uni- versity education that became one of his many influential books, The Idea of a University. Despite Cardinal Manning’s denunciation of Newman to Rome, he became a cardinal himself in 1879. In Portrait, Stephen names him “the greatest writer” of prose, an estimation set in shocking juxtaposition with his choice for the greatest writer of poetry, the “heretic,” the “immoral” Byron. This estimation is Joyce’s own, as the scene, set in Belvedere College, supposedly reproduces a conver- sation Joyce had when a student there. Joyce, like Stephen, reserves his highest admiration here for English writers. Certainly the culture in Clongowes and Belvedere would have been snobbishly Anglophilic, including the playing of English games such as rugby, a “gentlemanly” sport in contrast to the “savagery” of Davin’s game, hurling. Hurling was associated with the lower classes and with benighted country people, as was attending a Christian Broth- ers school where the sport was played. When Stephen’s father (like Joyce’s) speaks of “Paddy Stink and Mickey Mud,” he is referring to the Christian Brothers. Joyce deviates from following the pattern of his own education in Stephen’s story in one crucial detail—Stephen does not even briefly attend a Christian Brothers school. This disavowal of those Irish qualities associated with an “ignorant,” rustic past emerges as fear cast in tentatively Oedipal terms, terms that Stephen fails to sus- tain with any conviction; one of the journal entries that conclude the novel describes an old man encountered by one of Stephen’s friends when touring the west of Ireland. The old man is “in a mountain cabin.” He speaks Irish as well as English, “about universe and stars”: 64 Critical Insights

I fear him. I fear his redrimmed horny eyes. It is with him I must struggle all through this night till day come, till he or I lie dead, gripping him by the sinewy throat till . . . Till what? Till he yield to me? No. I mean him no harm. Many critics quote the lines near the closing of Portrait about Stephen forging “the uncreated conscience of [his] race,” but this is not the sen- tence that concludes the novel. The text concludes with the cry, “Old father, old artificer, stand me now and ever in good stead.” While Ste- phen’s biological father carries the name of the mythological artificer, Dedalus, there are other father figures present in the novel. Tone, Parnell, even Newman are all “artificers” of Stephen’s, and Ireland’s, “uncreated conscience.” The novel’s final plea, then, rejects the fear and violence of Stephen’s earlier reaction to “the old man.” The past, all fathers, must be acknowledged and honored in order to forge the always uncreated future.
