Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim Albert Wachtel George Noel Gordon, Lord Byron, is identified by Stephen Dedalus in the second chapter of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man as “the greatest poet.” Why Byron, one wonders, instead of a more talented contemporary—or Shakespeare for that matter? There is more than verse involved here. Like Stephen’s creator and model, Byron is a re- bel whose works are inseparable from his personal history. If James Joyce’s brother Stanislaus, Richard Ellmann, Joyce’s major biogra- pher, and Stephen Dedalus can be trusted, Byron inspired Joyce. The relationships between James Augustine Aloysius Joyce and Byron start with imposing names and issue through mawkish early poems into a mature commitment to creative honesty about conventionally disapproved behaviors that transcend even the facts. Their creative honesty transcends facts because both Joyce and By- ron present exacerbated versions of their troubled lives, often aug- menting the misdeeds and anguish of disguised semblances of them- selves. At Byron’s best, his defiance of authority and impenitent though not unregretful autobiographical bent are models for Joyce. As mature artists, both celebrate heightened truths about themselves, even as their works disapprove some of their impulses and deeds. When Joyce’s comatose mother was dying, James and Stanislaus turned away their uncle’s demand that they kneel and pray. No mistake there, many would say. But in unrepresented time between Joyce’s Por- trait and Ulysses Stephen Dedalus’s dying mother herself begs him to kneel. Stephen, a nonbeliever, refuses. She dies denied—“beastly dead,” Stephen’s friend Buck Mulligan observes without considering the rele- vance of his words to what Stephen has done. Whatever the many say about virtuous honesty and condemnable hypocrisy, denying his mother tortures Stephen, and he has troubled dreams about her. Unlike beasts, decent people indulge the dying. His honorable opposition to hypocrisy dishonors him, and that double perspective has a name: irony. 66 Critical Insights

Sometimes irony satirizes, exposing foibles and prejudices that should be abandoned. Sometimes it sarcastically attacks through scornful agreement with or understatement of what is abhorred. In A Portrait’s last chapter, Stephen, appalled by his beloved E. C.’s rela- tionships with other young men, thinks of her home as “the house where young men are called by their christian [sic] names a little too soon.” But sometimes irony reveals complexity, the inadequacy of simplistic saws. Like Cordelia’s innocent refusal to bend the truth to support her father’s political scheme at the outset of King Lear, Ste- phen’s commitment to personal integrity at his mother’s deathbed proves destructive as well as naively admirable. This third type of irony often requires sophisticated readers. Ironi- cally, at the end of A Portrait, when Stephen invokes as father and asks aid of the mythological first artist, Daedalus, young Dedalus inadver- tently links himself to Daedalus’s son Icarus, who irresponsibly flew too high with his father’s wings. The sun melted them, dropping him to his death. Readers who miss the point but read Ulysses find that, look- ing back, Stephen explicitly identifies himself as Icarus. Byron too gets things wrong as a youth and flies too high, and Joyce knew well that the great Romantic sometimes exemplifies what poets should not do. Byron first comes into prominence in Joyce’s publica- tions in the short story “A Little Cloud” as author of the timid protago- nist’s favorite poem, “On the Death of a Young Lady.” Little Chandler, already married and supporting a family, aspires to be a poet and loves that puerile first effort in Byron’s Hours of Idleness. In the first line, “evening gloom” has become as “still” as “HUSH’D” winds, as if gloom were sometimes noisy and hushed needed noisy capitalization, with a poetical apostrophe replacing unpronounced E to declare that the silent letter is not pronounced. Within two lines the young lady is both dust and clay. Her virtuous life is “unredeemed,” but Angels, cry- ing despite her salvation, welcome her into heaven. Byron’s note in the Poetical Works (reissued in 1904, two years before Joyce completed the story) confirms that Chandler’s taste is poor. Byron asks the Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 67

reader’s indulgence for this flawed first attempt at verse, written when he was fourteen years old. It stands unrevised for historical reasons. Like Chandler, Stephen—with the crucial difference that is he young—is moved by Byron’s juvenile lyrics. His schoolboy attempts at verse draw on Byron’s callow efforts to such an extent that the very titles of Byron’s poems strike him as worth imitating. Of course when Byron, anticipating the mature Joyce, abjures sani- tized saws, lays his intimate feelings open, and thus enlarges the field of human life available for appreciation, condemnation, or both, he is admirable. Joyce’s admiration of this iconoclasm outlives his youth. Ellmann tells us that after Ulysses made Joyce famous, Joyce wanted to produce Byron’s play Cain as an opera. The appreciation is as conceptual as it is aesthetic. In “Drama and Life,” about as old as Stephen is in the last chapter of A Portrait, Joyce describes drama as “the interplay of passions to por- tray truth.” In Stephen Hero, an early draft of A Portrait, Dedalus de- livers to angry classmates and professors a version of the paper, wed- ded to Joyce’s tribute to James Clarence Mangan. But Joyce omits the scene in A Portrait, keeping his aspiring artist immature. “We must ac- cept [life] as we see it,” Joyce asserts in his essay, relegating beauty to a secondary position. Byron reveals his intimate desires and activities, some of which—though shared by many—are hypocritically denied by the conventional at the cost of improved understanding of human- ity. From ordinary biological functions such as urinating (“When you wet the bed first it is warm then it gets cold,” toddler Stephen thinks on the first page of A Portrait) to deeply troubling decisions such as deny- ing one’s mother’s last wish, Joyce’s largely autobiographical art- ist-in-the-making struggles through experience toward what is true. Properly, Joyce and Byron, though they sometimes regard their im- pulses as ugly, are more opposed to misrepresenting them than they are to exposing personal moral failures through thinly veiled autobiographical personae. Like Joyce, Byron, though regarded as quintessentially Romantic, 68 Critical Insights

views the world as well as himself and his work ironically. Childe Har- old’s Pilgrimage, his book-length travel poem, reaches back for meter and rhyme to the complex nine-line Faerie Queene stanza of Edmund Spenser, rhyming ababbcbcc, the first eight lines in iambic pentameter and the ninth in hexameter, a length called alexandrine. The most ac- complished and serious narrative poet of the English Renaissance, without a hint of comedy, Spenser probably derived the stanza from the medieval rhyme royal of Geoffrey Chaucer, which the mature Chaucer mocks for its complexity in “The Tale of Sir Topas” of The Canterbury Tales. The Spenserian stanza, with its technical difficul- ties, implicitly asserts that its poem is very important. William Words- worth uses it in “The Female Vagrant,” written in first person from the point of view of the protagonist, and with either unintended comic lack of candor or patting himself on the back for skillfully masking the complex arrangement, Wordsworth observes in parentheses, “(The woman thus her artless story told).” Spenserian stanzas artless? That’s how she speaks? Ha! Byron, in part perhaps mocking his high-minded contemporary, delightfully begins Childe Harold with a Spenserian stanza that ironically renounces pretension. He calls on a heavenly muse to dismiss her. Childe Harold’s Pil- grimage, he avers, is not an epic. Of course, the denial of a muse at- tacks poetical presumption generally, and beyond Wordsworth’s af- fected simplicity and ambitious Spenser, who thought of his poem as the great English epic and himself as the English Vergil, the rejection of a “heavenly muse” specifically recalls John Milton, who undertakes in Paradise Lost to justify God’s decisions and invokes the capital H “Heavenly Muse” for help. Byron summons his lowercase version to tell her that she will not be needed. Joyce’s attack on epic pretension, like Byron’s, comes at the start of an epical autobiographical work, Ulysses. Irreverent Buck Mulligan pretends he is a priest and sets about converting his shaving lather into Christ’s body and blood. Unsurprisingly, he fails. Like Childe Harold, Ulysses proceeds without heavenly inspiration. Both Byron and Joyce Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 69

bristle with critical and comic ironies that skewer other writers and so- cial, political, and religious leaders, practices, and values as well as themselves, reveling in the contradictions that characterize their autobiographically significant protagonists. The rejection of the muse having been accomplished in the first stanza of Childe Harold, the second begins with the word “Whilome,” which (with an extra e to poke fun at Spenser’s attempt to imitate the archaic spellings of Chaucer) means, “Once upon a time,” the first words of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, which begins with a story toddler Stephen’s father tells. Stephen’s and Byron’s lives are related inversely: reversing Ste- phen’s (and Joyce’s) childhood experience of descent from eldest son of landed gentry to destitute offspring of a financial failure, Byron is romantically rescued from destitution, inheriting a title as well as the wealth that comes with it, what poor children dream of experiencing. At ten, after a deprived boyhood in Scotland, Byron inherits his uncle’s baronial estate. Suddenly affluent, his widowed mother—claiming de- scent from the Renaissance Scottish king James VI, who becomes James I of England—moves to London. She enrolls Byron in En- gland’s best schools, but he, romantically committed to dissipation and generosity, continues as lord and successful poet to pile up debts. Con- vinced that nobility requires him to donate royalties to charity, he dispenses his wealth and remains romantically liable. Also romantically, though handsome and grandly athletic, Byron is afflicted with a clubfoot, which was further damaged by a quack physi- cian who tortured him when he was a boy with useless treatments. Less romantically, he tends to obesity. He fights his weight with agonizing diets and purgatives. He is a splendid horseman, cricket player, boxer, and swimmer, but his clubfoot and battles with flesh darken his life. Women throw themselves at him, but he is in love with a half sister, Augusta Leigh, and attracted to men, including an ill-starred love for a Greek youth at the end of his life. On the Continent, his troubles and contradictions seem magnificent. 70 Critical Insights

The quintessential Romantic is a kind of Icarus who flies too high and is thus doomed. Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, the lengthy autobio- graphical travel poem that declares itself not to be epical, is a windfall success. In his preface, Byron points out that childe is a medieval term for the eldest son of nobility who has not yet attained knighthood. The eldest nephew of a childless nobleman, Byron retrospectively lays im- plicit claim to the title at a distance of some five hundred years. His poem of adventurous contemporary travels takes on the colors of me- dieval romance, the very source of the word “Romantic.” Stephen Dedalus romantically takes grandly troubled Byron, whose experience with poverty reverses his own, as his model. Irrepressively ironic and contradictory, however, Romantic Byron ties his verse to the origin of the term “romantic” ironically, eschewing grandeur and ad- miring eighteenth-century Enlightenment and its quintessential poet, the physically challenged Alexander Pope. As for Byron’s romantic commitment to liberty, four years before the freedom-loving nobleman dies while preparing to fight for Greek liberation, he writes “When a Man Hath No Freedom to Fight for at Home,” a satiric attack on people who set about fighting for the freedom of foreigners. Joyce’s life too is filled with contradictions. They begin with con- flicted names. His given names hark back—with telling ironies—to central figures of Christianity, but with clear contradictions in their history and application to Joyce. There is an odd irony in the life of James the Just, the first of several notable Christians who bear Joyce’s first name. That James is identi- fied in the New Testament as Jesus’ brother. After the crucifixion he leads Jesus’ Jewish followers in Jerusalem. But, despite his religious stature, Roman Catholic leaders, intent on keeping Jesus’mother a life- long virgin, reject the idea of physical brotherhood, arguing that James the Just is Jesus’ spiritual brother or cousin, the child of Mary’s sister Mary. That issue aside, ironically the name is also shared with Byron’s putative ancestor James I, king of the oppressive English in the life- time of William Shakespeare, and with Dublin’s St. James’s Gate Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 71

Brewery, where Guinness Stout has been distilling “spirits” since 1759. Objectively accidental but psychologically taken as causal, with “psychocausal” significance for Joyce, then, some religious accounts claim James the Just was stoned to death, martyrdom later attributed to Saint Stephen, the “first martyr,” whose name Joyce, thinking too of Stephen’s Green, the location of University College, which he attended as an undergraduate, took for Dedalus. Joyce, believer turned atheist, owes his second name to Saint Au- gustine, pagan turned Christian. Like Joyce’s Stephen, Augustine at one point turns down his mother’s plea that he embrace Christianity. After converting to Catholicism, he promotes the idea that the Church is the City of God, even as Joyce after abandoning the faith asserts that Dublin represents all modern cities. Ironically, another Augustine in the sixth century converts Ireland’s hated conquerors, the English, to Catholicism. A source of Joyce’s third given name, Aloysius Gonzaga, joins the Jesuits very young, distinguishes himself intellectually, and at age twenty-three dies into eventual sainthood while ministering to victims of the plague. A prime example of dedication and obedience—which the militant order’s creator and first “Superior General,” Ignatius Loyola, values most, specifying in his thirteenth rule that Jesuits should believe white black if the Holy See declares it to be so—Aloysius is the patron saint of Clongowes Wood College. Joyce, trained there, rejects the order, Aloysius-like turns to medicine but re- jects that, too, and utterly disobedient writes books that attack Jesuits and Church for their destructive attributes. Anticipatorily complex, Byron, in his life and in his works, is both a crucial figure of Romanticism and one who calls for its end. His sat- ires, beginning with English Bards and Scotch Reviewers and ending with Don Juan, attack central elements of the Romantic movement. His athleticism and the physically powerful characters in his po- etry—the inverse of the physically slight Joyce and his even less able fictional persona, Stephen Dedalus, who early in A Portrait of the Art- 72 Critical Insights

ist as a Young Man skirts the margins of a playing field because he is too weak to compete with his fellows and, like his creator, is afflicted with bad eyesight—contrast sharply with Byron’s own physical ills as well. But the image of Byron’s manliness remains an ideal for his lion- izers. Byron dives into dark night waters in Italy to save his friend and fellow poet, Percy Bysshe Shelley, providing another touchstone of Byronic heroism. Romantically intent on fighting for Greek indepen- dence from Turkey, Byron supplies arms, travels to Greece, and trains a militia, determined to fight for freedom against the Turks. Though he dies in his tent without ever seeing battle, he is embraced by the Greeks as a hero. Inversely, Stephen Dedalus is reluctant even to bathe, and though Joyce/Stephen seek political independence, they do so individually. Joyce dies a pacifist in Switzerland, which declared neutrality in World War II. Still, as Joyce felt obliged to leave Ireland, Byron left England, both of them almost never to return. Their parallels multiply. Preyed upon as a child by his nursemaid and addicted to prostitution, Byron is anal- ogous to Joyce/Stephen, who as a youth encounters sexually predatory priests and falls into adventures with prostitutes. Those experiences convince Stephen that he is bestial and doomed in the third chapter of A Portrait. Though Byron’s elevation to peerage romantically reverses the experience of Joyce, both are impecunious, serially in debt, and of- fensive to the conventional. Both, having been poor, sympathize with the poor. When Byron comes into control of his peerage he argues for the poor against the nobility in the House of Lords. Joyce, like Stephen in A Portrait, squanders what money he wins in writing contests on ex- travagant expenditures and spends much of his adult life in debt, writing about ordinary folk at the lip of poverty. Socially, Byron is a happy gifted conversationalist, but he claims to hate company and shuns gatherings. He condemns immorality and hy- pocrisy while declaring his undying incestuous love for his half sister, something he both celebrates and laments retrospectively in his play Manfred. Joyce also addresses incest, in his case prospectively in the Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 73

postmodernist Finnegans Wake, where a Dublin barkeep’s desire for his daughter is hidden in mythological, geographical, folk, and tempo- ral history and further obscured in a language compounded of many, with multifariously significant puns such as “insect” for “incest.” Less timid, Byron, through Manfred, a model of Romantic excesses, embraces and attacks incest clearly, and his satires attack Romantics directly, favoring neoclassicism. His verse ranges from juvenile love poems through poems of passionate excess to Enlightenment-inspired satires. Joyce has Stephen write many poems in the course of A Por- trait, beginning as a toddler with his adaptation of an already adapted version of H. S. Thompson’s “Lily Dale” in which protective adults in Stephen’s life have replaced Lily’s “green grave” with a “green place.” Toddler Stephen’s desire to get things right—though impeded by his imperfect recollection as well as the false rendering of those who al- tered the poem for him—is, like his accurate observation about wetting the bed, the stuff of which honorable art is made. Those examples of what poets should be doing and what stands in their way are balanced by Stephen’s misused art. His teenage ventures into love poetry fail. As we have seen, young Byron also writes love poems. One, “To E——,” serves as a model for Stephen’s title, “To E—— C——.” “It was right to begin so for he had seen similar titles in the collected poems of Lord Byron.” The influ- ence is destructive. Both efforts avoid the truth. Byron’s is decked out in poetical personifications, the stuff Wordsworth insightfully dis- missed in his 1802 “Preface to Lyrical Ballads.” Byron’s poem invites “Folly” to smile mockingly at the lower-class beloved’s name because Folly will be defeated. Capital V “Virtue” deserves greater love than “rank” (cleverly denied a capital). The poet acknowledges his “title deck’d . . . higher worth” and her “unequal . . . fate,” but asserts that her “modest worth” should be proud. The poem reeks of outdated usage and condescension, and the withholding of the beloved’s name turns the effort into a sham. Why is she unnamed if the brave nobleman thinks her worthy? 74 Critical Insights

A Portrait offers no evaluation of Stephen’s verse, but the experi- ence that leads to it is splendidly captured in the prose that precedes it. Stephen finds himself on a tram with E. C. Standing on the exit stairs, she flirts, playfully stepping up to his level and back down again. He takes her actions to be an invitation to embrace and kiss but is not bold enough. Moved to write about the experience, Stephen omits every- thing relevant. Instead he places lovers in a conventional romantic night in which they do kiss. We later learn the girl’s first name, Emma. A splendidly characterized Emma Clery inhabits Stephen Hero, but both last name and detailed characterization are absent from Portrait. Is it mere chance or psychocausal for Stephen that in Byron’s early Hours of Idleness there is a poem “To Emma” to whom the speaker bids “the fondest, last adieu”? Was Stephen in A Portrait attracted to his Emma, as much by the shared name as by her own qualities? Is that why the name Clery was left out? Joyce clearly wants us amused by the gap between the tram ride and Stephen’s poem—sympathetically. Un- ripe Stephen, infatuated with titles and names in Byron’s immature love poems, is not equal to young adult life. The narrative spares us the exact words of his poem, but the clichéd paraphrase assures us that it is a failure. Lovers kiss all the time. What justifies this version of the ex- perience, especially in light of the poem’s source, an opportunity missed? Stephen’s effort gives substance to a lie. Though Childe Harold, with its renunciation of epic presumptions, is about recognizable experiences, there is a precedent even in Byron’s mature verse for Stephen’s tendency to detach his poems from the real world. Manfred is engaged in disengaging from life, trying to forget his incestuous love for his deceased sister, Astarte, who shares a name with the pagan Semitic goddess of sexual love and fertility. Manfred’s sister was so splendid that (without a hint of comedy) she looked and sounded like him (2.2.107). No wonder he was in love with her! In mourning, seized by guilt, Manfred aspires to forgetfulness, but nei- ther his Faust-like quests for knowledge that transcends memory nor the “mysterious agency” of spirits frees him. Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 75

The problems Stephen Dedalus faces in the second chapter of A Portrait, masturbating and frequenting prostitutes, are less extreme than Manfred’s but devastating to him. Maddened by a guilt exacer- bated by the sermons he hears in the third chapter, he confesses and gains absolution from a kindly Christian brother, but he does not write about those experiences. What inspires him to verse is his failure to trust his sense that E. C. wants him to embrace and kiss her (which his poem lies about) and, in the last chapter, his jealousy of her playfulness with others. The “Villanelle of the Temptress,” the creative effort that follows upon Stephen’s jealousy, is not only presented; its composition is re- corded. The title declares its type, villanelle, a nineteen-line, two-rhyme French form that, like the Spenserian stanza, relishes its difficulty. Five three-line stanzas, in which the first and third lines all rhyme, as do the second lines of each stanza, are followed by a four-line sixth stanza of which the second line rhymes with the preced- ing seconds and the first, third, and fourth match the odd-line rhymes. As if that were not enough, the first and third lines of stanza one are re- peated alternately as the last line of the four remaining triplets and then constitute the last two lines of the poem. To his credit, Stephen manages to fulfill the requirements of the form while composing actual sentences. What is more, it has been ob- served that the word “villanelle” can be read as a female form of “vil- lain,” and since the woman addressed is regarded negatively—as someone who villainously caused the fall of angels and has enjoyed being courted ardently—it can be said that there are relationships among the poem’s form, title, and content, but beyond that cleverness the relationships are not illuminating. How does the situation in the poem relate to jealous Stephen and attractive E. C., who (we learn in the story’s prose rather than in Stephen’s verse) enjoys his singing and flirts? The poem’s words bring us no closer to an appreciation of Ste- phen’s situation than we were without them. His reference to fallen ser- aphim derives from Byron’s reading in Manfred of the perplexing 76 Critical Insights

verse of Genesis (6:4) in which “the sons of God went in to the daugh- ters of men, and they brought forth children,” the Nephalim or giants of old. Manfred refers to “the giant sons/ Of the embrace of angels with a sex/ More beautiful than they, which did draw down/ The erring spir- its who can ne’er return” (3.2.3-8). Linking Stephen’s young woman to Byron’s “more beautiful” sex of old, the villanelle’s “I” asks her if, having lured high-ranking angels, the “fallen seraphim,” and having been praised with poems that amount to “one eucharistic hymn,” she is not tired of “ardent ways,” all the attention that she is getting. The lines tell us little beyond those “hymns” about the nature of the ardent ways or the attractive, flirtatious young woman with whom Stephen is con- cerned; nor, for that matter, do they yield insight into the “enchanted days”—“tell no more” of them—that should no longer be spoken of. The process of composition does not help, either with understand- ing or appreciation, except perhaps with the deflating information that, inspired, Stephen woke up with his soul “dewy wet.” Wet with what? Dew does not fall on indoor beds, and where exactly is the soul lo- cated? Is it wet with sweat? Wet from Stephen having urinated in his bed as he did when a toddler? Something else? The moisture is cer- tainly not dew, and neither Stephen nor any of the young men with whom E. C. flirts is a fallen seraph. Moreover, Byron’s reading of the biblical passage, based on a first-century misinterpretation, most avail- able in New Testament Jude (6), is wrong. No angels fall and the sons of God are never identified as angels in the Hebrew Bible. Medieval Jewish theologians identify the sons as “of God” because they are de- scended from Adam’s honorable son Seth, born after Cain slew Abel, and take the passage to mean that Seth’s male descendents had sex with Cain’s female progeny—also an imposition on the text, but one that avoids the creation of a major supportive event like the fall of angels that does not exist there. Stephen’s poem—like the representation of Manfred, an over-the-mountaintop conversant with spirits who explores all ave- nues of knowledge in an attempt to escape suffering—fails to address Joyce, Byron, and the Fall of Seraphim 77

human experience directly. Byron is thus a twofold inspiration. As one who boldly sets out to live in defiance of religious and social norms, to write about passions deemed unacceptable, one who critiques his time in witty satires and has his protagonist, Manfred, powerfully reject both heaven and hell, refusing to be damned or saved, Byron is a posi- tive inspiration. But he is also an example of bad writing, the kind of thing that Little Chandler loves and that Stephen has to grow beyond. At his best, Byron is a kind of Daedalus for Joyce, a great artificer, some of whose work is sexually challenging. But the autobiographical creations of Byron and Joyce are also Icarus-like. The two are seraphic high fliers who plunge down, “overreachers” who, rejecting all re- straint in their quest for the liberty afforded by the true, fall. Ironically, both Joyce and Byron found versions of that true in everyday life. In Manfred the protagonist is saved from what looks like the brink of suicide by a Chamois Hunter, a poor decent man who takes the in- comparable sinner to his home and nurses and feeds him. Manfred, be- yond the poor man’s ken, understands—Wordsworth-like—that the life of the Chamois Hunter is best. The Chamois Hunter will die at peace, loved by his grandchildren, a fitting epitaph. But he has a small part in the play. In Ulysses, Joyce centrally celebrates and Stephen meets a modern version of such a man. Loving, misunderstood, decent, generous, and devoted, the advertising salesman Leopold Bloom, who takes Stephen to his home, is Joyce’s mock and serious hero, a man whose foibles amuse and whose virtues exceed those of the heroes of old. “Odysseus blinded the Cyclops,” I wrote in The Cracked Lookingglass; “Bloom tries to give the Citizen he confronts new vision.” Back in Ireland again when Ulysses starts, still shy of the great artist who immortalizes Bloom, Stephen mocks his own fervor as A Portrait ends when, fleeing to Paris, he takes the mythological Daedalus as his inspiration. Stephen there plans to “forge [create? falsify?] the conscience of his race.” In Ulysses he meets and is helped by an everyday model of decency and good conscience, suggesting to those who like to read beyond the last 78 Critical Insights

words of books that someday Stephen/Joyce will write Bloom’s story, surpassing both his efforts as a young man and those of his hero Byron. “By Dint of Brooding on the Incident”: Professional Readers’ Responses to A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man Parker Douglas James Joyce (1882-1941) is arguably the most influential fiction writer of the twentieth century. His influence on the techniques of writ- ers, ranging from traditional realists to the most wildly experimental postmodernists, is unquestionable and decisive. Although Joyce’s Ulysses (1922) has elicited a larger amount of critical discussion and response, there can be no doubt that A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) is Joyce’s most widely read work apart from individual stories found in his collection Dubliners (1914). While Portrait is among the most frequently taught “modernist” novels, it is also a novel that undergraduates and high school students often discover on their own. In spite of its surface difficulties, young readers, and serious readers of all ages, still respond to the work’s uncanny and convincing portrayal of a sensitive youth who is harrowed by religious and sexual guilt and is in the process transfigured by an idea of beauty—a com- mon trope in so-called modernist literature. The remarkable self- involvement of the protagonist, Stephen Dedalus, and his frustration under the authority of Church, state, and family resonate for all youthful in age and temperament, however different the specifics of circumstance. Portrait is nevertheless usually encountered seriously. In a much-discussed, if controversial, 1997 Random House poll, Joyce’s Ulysses was named the number one novel of the twentieth century, and Portrait was named the third, behind F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby. This surely adds a different kind of heft to the book when the reader first picks it up. Whether enthusiastic about the endeavor or not, every reader of Joyce’s Portrait starts out innocent, wishing to be oth- erwise, aware that there are meanings somewhere presupposed. In rel- ative kind, readers might take some comfort in the fact that their first 80 Critical Insights

encounter in reading the novel is not wholly unlike the trajectory of Stephen’s experience in the novel. Portrait has variously been claimed to be both an example and an ironic criticism of the bildungsroman (novel of education and maturation) and its close relative the Künstlerroman (which focuses on the development of the artist); any account of coming to terms with Portrait might therefore rightly be considered a “Leserroman” or “Lektorroman,” to butcher but never- theless coin a German term—a story of readers or lecturers making meaning. It is the aim of this essay to offer such innocents, of whom I was happily once one, possible paths in the form of an incomplete, though fair in purpose, account of the novel’s treatment in previous criticism, in order that reading innocents might, if they so choose, forge—to use a central image from Portrait itself—their own meanings in their encounter with Joyce’s novel. Initial Responses to the Novel So well established is Portrait as a modern classic that it is difficult to imagine the situation of the novel’s early reviewers, faced with a writing of the sort they had not encountered before, the closest ana- logues in the English tongue being Robert Browning’s or T. S. Eliot’s interior monologues, although William Wordsworth’s lyrics also are a neglected artistic predicate influence. Spotting literary greatness is dif- ficult when one is encountering true innovation on its first appearance. While Ezra Pound certainly did recognize greatness in Joyce, as did Eliot, even as perceptive a reader as Edward Garnett, who had earlier encouraged Joseph Conrad, Ford Madox Ford, and D. H. Lawrence, balked at Joyce’s work. In a reader’s report for the publisher Duck- worth & Co., collected with many other reviews in Robert H. Dem- ing’s two-volume James Joyce: The Critical Heritage (1970), Garnett observed that the novel is “ably written” but needs revision because it is too “discursive, formless, unrestrained, and ugly things, ugly words, are too prominent.” The work is too “unconventional,” Garnett opined, Professional Readers’ Responses 81

and “unless the author will use restraint and proportion he will not gain readers” (81). While possibly not a totally inaccurate estimation of the work’s ca- pacity to gain popularity among the masses, this aesthetic misjudg- ment by a usually canny reader is somewhat unexpected, and it is all the more surprising that so many of the initial reviews of Portrait hailed it as a literary landmark, even a work of “genius,” a label more than sometimes only parsimoniously bestowed by fellow craftsmen. For instance, Pound’s review in The Egoist, where the book had ap- peared in installments, stressed that it was well crafted—and Pound tried to suggest just how rare that was among novels in English. In- deed, “Joyce produces the nearest thing to Flaubertian prose that we now have in English.” Aside from that, “I doubt if a comparison of Mr. Joyce to other English writers or Irish writers would help much to de- fine him.” Pound stressed Joyce’s realism and the novel’s value as “di- agnosis,” but otherwise said virtually nothing about the novel’s con- tent (in Deming 83). Others were more struck by what they saw as the work’s unpleasantness. A review in Everyman titled “A Study in Gar- bage” called it “an astonishingly powerful and extraordinary dirty study of the upbringing of a young man by Jesuits” and suggested that at the end of the book Stephen goes mad (in Deming 85). Similarly, H. G. Wells, in a rather awestruck essay comparing Joyce to Jonathan Swift, Laurence Sterne, and Joseph Conrad, nevertheless complained about Joyce’s “cloacal obsession” (in Deming 86-88). The Times pro- tested the “occasional improprieties”; the Literary World complained of “the brutal probing of the depths of uncleanness” and the Manches- ter Guardian of the novel’s “astounding bad manner” (in Deming 89, 92, 93). What surely is described here is Portrait’s participation in a central feature of modernism, which, as many critics have traditionally observed, shocked some readers of the time out of convention (Gay 197-98). Like other reviewers, the Guardian’s critic found in Stephen “a pas- sion for foul-smelling things” (in Deming 93), confusing Joyce’s par- 82 Critical Insights

ticularly acute technique of documenting odors and textures with his protagonist’s actual tastes. Irish reviewers were, if anything, more of- fended than British ones. The Freeman’s Journal claimed that “Mr. Joyce plunges and drags his readers after him into the slime of foul sewers” (in Deming 98). These critics’ stress on Portrait’s early kitchen-sink realism is likely to be somewhat baffling to contemporary readers until we recognize that the “impropriety” found on the book’s “very first page” (in Deming 89) can only be the reference to bed- wetting; and at this point we understand what a large part of human ex- perience was held to be inappropriate in 1916 Europe for literary treatment. One theme not picked up in later criticism is the concern over whether Stephen and his companions are representative of Irish youth in their ideas. Wells noted that “every human being” in the book “ac- cepts as a matter of course . . . that the English are to be hated” and adds that he thinks that picture is “only too true” (in Deming 88). The Free- man’s Journal, on the other hand, protested that “English critics, with a complacency that makes one despair of their intelligence, are already hailing the author as a typical Irishman, and his book as a faithful pic- ture of Irish life.” It would be just as accurate to see Thomas De Quincey’s Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1822) as a typical picture of British youth, the reviewer—perceptive, defensive, humorous—asserts (in Deming 99). Still, Joyce’s technique was so convincing that the reviewers had to admit that something beyond conventional realism was at work. A. Clutton-Brock said that “[Joyce] can make anything happen that he chooses” in writing, and that “no living writer is better at conversa- tion” (in Deming 89). J. C. Squire agreed that Joyce’s dialogue “is as close to the dialogue of life as anything I have ever come across” (in Deming 101). Virtually all near-contemporary reviewers praised the writing, and some were swept away in spite of themselves, protesting all the while. The Manchester Guardian’s writer began: “When one recognizes genius in a book one continues. . . . Not for its apparent Professional Readers’ Responses 83

formlessness should the book be condemned. A subtle sense of art has worked amidst the chaos, making this hither-and-thither record of a young mind and soul . . . a complete and ordered thing” (in Deming 92). In noting this he was unusual, for nearly all the early contempo- rary reviewers complained of the book’s formlessness, its abrupt tran- sitions, its seeming lack of plot, and its unusual demands upon the reader. Just as the term “naturalism” was used to evoke the “gutter real- ism” of the then-notorious Émile Zola, the term “impressionism” was frequently applied to Portrait to suggest an aesthetic combination of shapelessness and sensitivity in both protagonist and narrative. Early Attempts to Place Joyce’s Work Reaction to Portrait did not occur in a vacuum, both because, as dis- cussed above, serious literary contemporaries tried to evaluate the con- tribution of the work to literaria honestly and because within two years of its publication installments of Joyce’s even more challenging Ulys- ses began to appear in the Little Review. In a now-famous essay titled “Modern Novels” that appeared in 1919, Virginia Woolf hailed Joyce’s work as an example of a revolutionary sort of fiction that was challeng- ing outmoded conventions. “Let us record the atoms as they fall upon the mind in the order which they fall, let us trace the pattern, however disconnected and incoherent in appearance, which each sight or inci- dent scores upon the consciousness,” Woolf urged. In doing this—shifting the focus inward, toward momentary perceptions and a “spiritual” dimension of consciousness—Woolf asserted, the artist could produce something closer to “life itself” (in Deming 125-26). Gradually, at least within the serious literary community we have con- structed in hindsight, it began to be realized that a group of writers in- cluding Eliot, Pound, Joyce, and Woolf herself were engaged in similar challenges to the literary conventions of the day, and that the art of such writers demanded evaluation on its own terms rather than censure for departing from the norms of Victorian verse and prose. This had 84 Critical Insights

two effects: first, published commentary on the work of writers such as Joyce tended to become exclusively laudatory or exclusively deroga- tory, depending on which position the reviewer took in the politics of art; second, as comments by Joyce’s increasing circle of admirers appeared, those critics who took him seriously began devoting their energies to explicating his work rather than evaluating it. The arrival of Ulysses in 1922 certainly sharpened the aesthetic and political divide among literary critics just described more clearly than Portrait had done. Stuart Gilbert’s 1930 James Joyce’s “Ulysses,” written with Joyce’s help, revealed to an uninformed public the com- plexity of that work’s mythic structure, as well as the richness and vari- ety of its stylistic and narrative effects. One implication relative to this inquiry is that Portrait, or even the earlier collection Dubliners, might well have formal complexities of its own that, as with Ulysses, had gone unnoticed. Gilbert also stressed Joyce’s use of symbolism, a char- acteristic of his prose that Joyce’s early reviewers, more focused on his use of naturalistic detail, had slighted. Reviewers on the political left were little impressed with this formal preoccupation and innovation, especially during the reign of “social realism” in the 1930s; such re- viewers often dismissed Joyce as obscure, bourgeois, and apolitical. A Russian essay translated in New Masses (1933) found the stream-of-consciousness method of Ulysses to be “too closely con- nected with the ultra-subjectivism of the parasitic, rentier bourgeoisie, and entirely unadaptable to the art of one who is building a socialist so- ciety.” The naturalism of Portrait might at first seem more promising, since it exposes the material evils of capitalism, but it was said to have its roots in “a morbid, defeatist delight in the ugly and repulsive” and in “an aesthetic-proprietary desire for the possession of ‘things’” (in Deming 591-92). As for the portions of Work in Progress that had so far appeared in journals, the Marxist reviewer (like mainstream reviewers throughout Europe and the United States) dismissed them as nonsense. At the same time, another contemporary literary trend tended to Professional Readers’ Responses 85

support and favor Joyce. Increasingly during the twentieth century, Anglophone writers became aware of Continental literary tradi- tion—though surely not an altogether new feature of European literary culture, modernism’s cosmopolitan quality is frequently featured if not fetishized in criticism on the subject. In any case, in the 1920s both British and American writers migrated to Paris, often to sit at the feet of Joyce or Gertrude Stein, the great expatriates. Since Joyce’s literary models were generally European rather than British or Irish, his work was more intelligible and less frighteningly original when seen in this context. Indeed, Ulysses was probably the first important work of En- glish literature to be explicated and celebrated first by French critics. During the 1930s and 1940s a generation of American critics who were conversant with European literature naturally named Joyce among the great contemporary writers. Most notably, Edmund Wilson in his 1931 book Axel’s Castle placed Joyce in the literary tradition of the French Symbolist poets of 1870-90. The Natality of the Joyce Industry Probably the first serious study of Joyce’s writing as a whole—apart from early biographical studies and the writings of Joyce’s friends—was Harry Levin’s pioneering James Joyce: A Critical Intro- duction (1941). This remarkable book, much of it written when only portions of Finnegans Wake had appeared under the title Work in Prog- ress, is still one of the better introductions to Joyce’s work. Levin treats Portrait as autobiography and understands little irony in Joyce’s treat- ment of Stephen. Levin presents Portrait as a late example of the bil- dungsroman (such as Stendhal’s The Red and the Black or Gustave Flaubert’s A Sentimental Education). He briefly discusses Stephen’s aesthetic theory and suggests that the progression from the “lyric” to “epic” to “dramatic” forms characterizes Joyce’s work as a whole. Levin presents Joyce as heir to the two apparently opposed late nine- teenth-century strains of naturalism and symbolism, and argues that in 86 Critical Insights

Joyce, as in Flaubert, the two “come to terms.” In rather general terms he discusses the structural balance of the five chapters. Although most of his discussion in the book concerns Ulysses and Finnegans Wake, Levin does point out the dominant symbolic motif of flight and the role of the mythical Daedalus, the “fabulous artificer,” in Portrait. Anumber of other introductory works on Joyce were published dur- ing the 1940s, although not of Levin’s quality. One general study pub- lished during the 1950s that is still useful is Marvin Magalaner and Richard M. Kain’s Joyce: The Man, the Work, the Reputation (1956). These authors survey the early reviews as well and the serious criti- cism available up to then, and intelligently discuss the problem of Joyce’s biography, quoting from his then-unpublished letters. Their discussion of Portrait is particularly illuminating, as they compare Portrait with its first-draft version, a portion of which was published as Stephen Hero (1944). They stress the revision’s condensation, abrupt transitions, and impressionistic technique, and explore some of the references to obscure or popular works such as Edward Bulwer-Lytton’s play The Lady of Lyons (1838) and Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte-Cristo (1844). Most of their discussion centers on motifs such as apology, names, and blindness, and on the idea of epiphany and its function in the novel. They also single out for discussion the single most influential essay on Portrait at the time, Hugh Kenner’s “The Portrait in Perspective,” first published in 1948 and revised in his 1955 book Dublin’s Joyce. Kenner’s essay reads Portrait in light of Ulysses and Finnegans Wake and finds the work similar in complexities and implication. Where “the two major works strive toward inclusive mythopoetic vi- sion embracing in an archetypal pattern of fall, struggle, and redemp- tion every mode of human activity,” Portrait does this only on the level of individual human action, suggesting “other possible levels of anal- ogy” by implication. By pursuing these implications, Kenner shows how the novel’s first two pages “enact the entire action in microcosm.” He pursues the “verbal leitmotif” linking whiteness, cold, and damp as Professional Readers’ Responses 87

a repellant complex (as in the famous last scene of “The Dead”) and shows how words with their slippages and associations illustrate stages in Stephen’s development. Kenner argues that Stephen’s “epiphanies” that arrest and embody artistic meaning in a single mo- ment are not Joyce’s method; instead, in each chapter of the novel Joyce repeats the same pattern of showing Stephen embracing the dream in contempt of reality and then seeing the dream destroyed. “The movement of the book is dialectical; each chapter closes with a synthesis of triumph which in turn feeds the sausage-machine set up in the next chapter.” Most important, Kenner argues that “Stephen’s flight into adolescent ‘freedom’is not meant to be the ‘message’of the book.” Rather, Stephen, Kenner asserts, is an “indigestibly Byronic” figure, viewed ironically throughout. Contrasting directly with Levin’s assessment, Kenner finds Stephen’s rather Neoplatonic aesthetic is not Joyce’s; his Romanticism is scorned by the more classically minded Joyce; and instead of becoming the author of Portrait and Ulysses, Stephen will become a “parlor aesthete,” priggish, horrified by the sensual world, and egotistically self-involved. Although Kenner qualified his argument in later books and articles, his essay set the terms for the debate for many other critics for a gener- ation. The question is that of Joyce’s distance from his protagonist, and since the narrative voice itself changes greatly in the course of Por- trait, this is not at all a simple question—it is a creative one. In his criti- cal edition of Portrait (1968), Chester G. Anderson summarizes the de- bate and includes relevant essays by Wayne C. Booth and Robert Scholes. Booth’s essay, which originally appeared in his work The Rhetoric of Fiction, contends that the degree of Joyce’s irony—his “authorial distance”—cannot be established with any certainty be- cause Joyce at times clearly admires Stephen and at times clearly sati- rizes him. As Booth points out, the problem is epitomized by Stephen’s poem the “Villanelle of the Temptress”: it is unclear to many readers whether they are to take the poem as a success or as a failure. For Booth the problem is that Joyce was never certain of his own attitude toward 88 Critical Insights

his protagonist—the boy is self-deluded in his more grandiose mo- ments. The problem, according to Booth, is a flaw in Portrait itself. This argument is by no means settled—and this author would argue that the tension is centrally promoted and central to Joyce’s aesthetic itself, making him an inspiration to inspectors of indeterminate irony as diverse as Samuel Beckett, Thomas Pynchon, and Alain Robbe-Grillet—and it echoes down to the present day in Joyce criti- cism in debates, to take just one example, over whether Stephen’s mi- sogyny is also Joyce’s or whether it is being ironically displayed by a Joyce sympathetic to feminist concerns. The tension over Joyce’s and/or Stephen’s relationship to Byron and his work is productively explored in the new essay by Albert Wachtel in this volume. More critics contemporary with Kenner were less concerned with Joyce’s moral stance toward his hero than with the internal complexi- ties of his work. William York Tindall wrote three influential studies during the 1950s—James Joyce: His Way of Interpreting the Modern World (1950), A Reader’s Guide to James Joyce (1959), and The Joyce Country (1960)—all of which mingle Tindall’s flair for close, “New Critical” explication with his interest in literary symbolism and in the theories of Sigmund Freud. In his Reader’s Guide, Tindall begins by asserting that Stephen may not be Joyce, but he is indeed the artist- hero-rebel. True to the formalist assumptions of the New Critics, Tindall looks at four sections of chapters 1, 2, and 5 and the three sec- tions of chapters 3 and 4, and argues that while he is unsure of the func- tion of each part, “I am sure from what I know of Joyce that no part could be omitted or placed elsewhere without injuring the great de- sign” (62). True to the New Critical valuation of irony, as well as its faith in art as an organic unity (which it inherited, via Allen Tate, from Samuel Taylor Coleridge), Tindall catalogs some of the ironic juxtapo- sitions and echoes in the novel for the purpose of demonstrating the unity and purpose of its design. Like other formalists, Tindall is passionately interested in symbol- ism as well as structure, and, consequently, he spends a number of Professional Readers’ Responses 89

pages on the wings and labyrinth built by the mythical Daedalus (ech- oed by Stephen’s imaginative “flights” and the maze of Dublin streets), not to mention the sexual contrivance Daedalus made for Queen Pasiphae, a wooden cow with which she attracted a bull, and the “ro- bot” Talus he fashioned to protect Crete (neither of which, to Tindall’s chagrin, is present in Portrait). Tindall explores Stephen’s less sweep- ing identifications, with Jesus Christ (with Cranly playing John the Baptist, the “precursor”), Napoleon, Parnell, the Count of Mon- te-Cristo, the poet Dante, and Saint Stephen (the first Christian martyr) before lingering for a while on Lucifer (“bearer of light”), who like Stephen declares “I will not serve” and like Prometheus brings human- kind the forbidden fire of knowledge. Less significant than symbols, but also helping to unify the novel, motifs greatly interest Tindall. He finds on the opening pages road, cow, water, woman, flower, and bird, all of which will recur meaning- fully and, at least metaphorically, musically (Reader’s Guide 86). Other motifs, such as dogs, darkness and light, and the related blind- ness and sight, work similarly. Tindall “unpacks” a few of these im- ages, showing how birds can be threatening (Heron, the eagles), im- ages of escape (the birds above the library), or images of beauty (the wading “bird-girl” of Stephen’s epiphany in chapter 4). Birds also, of course, relate to the Daedalus myth. Similarly, the flower, a Neoplaton- ic symbol for the woman who exemplifies transcendent beauty and thus the poet’s path to the divine world, is complicated by Stephen’s in- vocation of an artificial “green rose” (surely an inspiration for Fitzger- ald’s “green light” in Gatsby, just as surely as Fitzgerald also identifies that light as problematically demonic as well as alluring and inspiring). The green rose relates also to the red/green opposition throughout the book: green suggests imagination, fertility, Ireland, and so on, while red suggests British authority, the Church, hellfire, and so forth. Of course, not all of these insights were unique to Tindall, but aside from his own contributions he conveniently and wittily synthesized the work of many scholars of the day for a generation of readers. 90 Critical Insights

Studies of the novel’s structure include Lee T. Lemon’s “A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man: Motif as Motivation and Structure” (1966), an analysis in- spired by the Russian Formalists, and Sidney Feshbach’s “A Slow and Dark Birth: A Study of the Organization of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man” (1967), which is more psychological in orientation. Other essays representative of work done in the 1950s and 1960s can be found in collections of essays on Portrait edited by Thomas E. Con- nolly (1962), William E. Morris and Clifford A. However, New Critical studies of the novel as self-contained struc- ture unified by symbols and motifs were not the only work done during this period—or even, in some respects, the most important Joyce scholarship produced at the time. The natural course of Joyce criticism was altered forever by the publication of Richard Ellmann’s magiste- rial biography James Joyce in 1959. Trained as a New Critic, Ellmann nonetheless “read” Joyce’s life as if it were a literary text. Given a writer whose life and work were as intimately intertwined as Joyce’s, Ellmann’s approach proved to be extremely convincing, especially as Ellmann skillfully interwove literary interpretation with biography throughout, a method not again approached until Albert Wachtel pro- duced The Cracked Lookingglass: James Joyce and the Nightmare of History in 1992. Stuart Gilbert had edited a collection of Joyce’s letters in 1957; in 1966 Ellmann reedited that volume and produced two addi- tional volumes. The sheer mass of information about Joyce, some of it quite intimate, was enough to make some critics forget about the dan- gers of the so-called biographical fallacy. Meanwhile, Robert Scholes Professional Readers’ Responses 91

For instance, the most influential essay treating Joyce’s actual composition process in writing Portrait is Hans Walter Gabler’s “The Seven Lost Years of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man” (1976). Sideways and Back: Joyce Criticism After Structuralism The 1970s, for better and worse, were characterized by the influ- ence on American and British criticism of a variety of Continental crit- ical approaches, most of which had been strenuously resisted during the previous decades. The so-called phenomenological criticism of the Geneva School, whose best American practitioner was the early J. Hillis Miller, was reflected in Joyce scholarship in Suzette Henke’s Joyce’s Moraculous Sindbook (1978), which deals with Ulysses, and R. B. Kershner’s “Time and Language in Joyce’s Portrait” (1976), a study of the interiority of Stephen’s time sense and the ways in which subjectivity and objectivity are unified in his experience. The Exile of James Joyce (1972), by Hélène Cixous—who later would be best known as a major “French feminist” theorist—combines a psychologi- cal approach to Joyce’s work as a whole with themes such as absence and silence or art as transgression that were of particular interest to structuralists and poststructuralists. Arenewed interest in Marxist criticism, especially as adapted by the “Frankfurt school” (and in socially and politically based criticism in general) led to a new distance from the society of which both Stephen and Joyce were a part. Issues such as Joyce’s sexual tastes now seemed less important in themselves and more significant as markers of social development at a given historical moment. James Naremore’s “Con- 92 Critical Insights

sciousness and Society in A Portrait of the Artist” (1976) discusses “some of the ways that Stephen Dedalus’s ideas, language, and art have been affected by his economic status and his Catholic upbring- ing,” and also reveals Joyce’s fictional technique as a variety of real- ism that betrays the author’s defensive reaction against his own “excremental vision.” The Godlike impersonality that Stephen claims for the artist, and that New Critics claimed for Joyce, was wearing thin. While Naremore asserts that Joyce was a more politically aware writer than most earlier critics thought, Richard Ellmann’s The Conscious- ness of Joyce (1977) provides evidence for the writer’s interest in poli- tics from Joyce’s own library. Joyce had early termed himself a social- ist and had referred to the change in relationship between women and men as the most important social change of his time; Ellmann demon- strates that Joyce’s political awareness was not simply a fashion of his youth. Dominic Manganiello’s full-scale study Joyce’s Politics (1980) broadens the argument, presenting Joyce as—unlike other major mod- ernists such as Yeats, Eliot, or Pound—a social progressive. During the 1970s and 1980s a host of historically responsive forms of criticism came into vogue, and with them a spectrum of interests that might once have seemed peripheral to Joyce’s art. Richard Brown’s James Joyce and Sexuality (1985) shows how the sexual rebellious- ness, oddity, or experimentation of Joyce’s characters occurs within a political and cultural context in which, for instance, assenting to con- ventional marriage could be understood as ceding control of one’s sex- uality to the state. Cheryl Herr’s groundbreaking Joyce’s Anatomy of Culture (1986) sets Joyce’s work within the context of the popular press, the popular theater, and the tradition of popular religious ora- tory, arguing that Joyce’s use of these materials produces a powerful social critique. R. B. Kershner’s Joyce, Bahktin, and Popular Litera- ture (1989), which treats Joyce’s early writing, makes a similar argu- ment from an analysis of the late nineteenth century and includes an extended discussion of Portrait. Meanwhile, structuralism, deconstruction, and poststructuralism Professional Readers’ Responses 93

began to have major impacts on Joyce studies. Relatively few of the Continental critics and their followers addressed Portrait directly, however, preferring to use (and that verb phrase is intentional) Ulysses and especially Finnegans Wake to exemplify the ways in which lan- guage itself forms complex structures independent of signification or alternately undermines itself. Starting in the 1970s, essays on Joyce by Roland Barthes and Jacques Derrida began appearing in Joyce confer- ence volumes. Books and articles devoted to Joyce studies looked to these and others in an attempt to prompt what many took to be a new theoretical vigor. Following Barthes’s famous but often misunderstood pronouncement of the “death of the author” as a locus of critical in- quiry in modern literary studies, the new work paid increased atten- tion—not so unlike the New Critics often reviled in more recent stud- ies—to style and structure in Joyce’s work, and especially to the linguistic and philosophical implications of these inquiries. Once again, the biographical was shunned in most of this work, and, in some, an exaggerated reading of Derrida’s critique of structuralism again exaggerated these critical tendencies. For a concrete example, the best book that exemplifies these trends, and applies them to Portrait as well, is Colin MacCabe’s post- structuralist James Joyce and the Revolution of the Word (1979). Sum- mary is difficult for a book like this. MacCabe refuses to “interpret” Joyce in any conventional sense: “Instead of constructing a meaning, Joyce’s texts concern themselves with the position of the subject in lan- guage” (4). While MacCabe also refuses to “psychologize” Joyce in any ordinary way, he does rely heavily on the work of Jacques Lacan, a revi- sionist Freudian who redirected attention to language as the primary ma- terial of the psychoanalytic method. Further, MacCabe insists that his reading of Joyce is radically political, because Joyce’s revolutionary politics are inherent in his language and its new relationship to represen- tation, rather than residing in any particular statements in his texts. MacCabe sees in the movement from Stephen Hero to Portrait a change from the ordered world of the “classic realist text,” in which 94 Critical Insights

meaning is guaranteed by a “Father” and resolution is implied by the very narrative, to a new world in which all meanings are provisionary, in which third and first person blend, and in which sound carries more weight than sense. Although the language of the artist threatens to estab- lish a “metalanguage”—apparently implying control or that all artistic persuasion or appreciation is nefarious to one’s political if not personal existence—that will enable us to evaluate the other languages repre- sented in the novel, even this possibility is frustrated by the novel’s dis- continuities. The technical problems that for critics like Booth had marked flaws in Portrait are precisely those that MacCabe celebrates as liberating us from the epistemology of bourgeois humanism. Whether or not one agrees that the aesthetic contains the seed for such political revolutionary tendencies (surely comforting to academ- ics who may wish to influence or believe they influence culture and politics outside the classroom), the general trend of criticism in the past two decades has been away from the New Critical presumption of or- ganic unity in Joyce’s works, away from symbolic interpretation, and in some ways away from biography. The stress has been on close anal- ysis of style, a reexamination of the social and political context of Joyce’s work, an intense theoretical examination of the implications of Joyce’s writing projects, and a questioning of previous interpretations of the entire modernist movement. An excellent relatively recent arti- cle that exemplifies at least some of these points is Michael Levinson’s “Stephen’s Diary in Joyce’s Portrait: The Shape of Life” (1985). The best example of a critic able to integrate Tindall’s ability to read closely while incorporating the best impulses of Kenner, Ellmann, and the inspirations of Continental criticism is Sean Latham’s excellent “Introduction: Joyce’s Modernities” (2010). Important work on Ulys- ses and, especially, Finnegans Wake has appeared under the stimulus of Continental approaches, and the fact that both Derrida and Lacan championed Joyce has encouraged a great deal of work indebted to contemporary Continental philosophical preoccupations. The collec- tion of politically oriented contemporary critical approaches, loosely Professional Readers’ Responses 95

grouped together under the labels “cultural criticism” and “New Historicism,” have also had an impact on Joyce studies, as described above. The most influential intellectual event in the humanities in the past thirty-plus years, the rise of feminist criticism, has also been re- flected in a wide variety of feminist approaches to Joyce as well. A fair question may be: To what end shall tomorrow’s reading of Joyce’s great novel exist? Of course, this question assumes that read- ing is something more than an end in itself. The answer is that new in- terpretations are inevitable if readers’ responses are worth communi- cating. As yet, we might ask if we have had an adequate description of the pure enjoyment that a first struggle with the novel provokes.
