Refining the Artist into Existence: Pygmalion’s Statue, Stephen’s Villanelle, and the Venus of Praxiteles Bonnie Roos Artists have written exhaustively on the mysterious powers of the artist and his creation with an introspective fascination that suggests their exploration is linked to the human condition. The concept of art coming to life, of an artistic work being in some fashion magically linked to its subject, dates back to the oldest mythologies of Western history. In a famous competition, the great artist Zeuxis reputedly painted grapes so real that birds flew to the image, deceived by it. Parrhasios, his competitor, painted only a broad curtain, which Zeuxis asked him to pull aside to reveal his work. Parrhasios was deemed the more talented for Zeuxis could fool birds, but Parrhasios could fool the artist himself.1 Sculpture too became magical when realistic. Legend has it that Myron sculpted a cow so real that bulls came from miles around to mate with it.2 Similarly, in a Euripides tale, the legendary ar- tificer Daedalus creates the perfect replica of a cow hollowed for Pasiphaë to enable her to satisfy her craving for a bull (Kris and Kurz 67). And the human sculptures of Daedalus, said to be the first sculp- tures with feet apart, arms loose and eyes open, needed to be fastened down, according to Plato’s account, to prevent them from walking away (67). The famous sculptor Praxiteles was said to have created a statue of a nude woman so beautiful that it inspired desire in every man who saw it. His statue, the Aphrodite of Knidos, a representation of the Greek goddess of love and fertility, may have inspired Ovid to write his story of Pygmalion. But whether or not Ovid’s telling of Pygmalion is related to the Knidian Aphrodite, the kinds of tensions between art and life that are articulated in both these stories merit closer examination. Christine Havelock devotes almost an entire book, The Aphrodite of Knidos and Her Successors (1995), to this single statue, significant be- Refining the Artist into Existence 307

cause it was unprecedented, the first female nude to be introduced in three-dimensional and monumental form.3 Havelock links the statue with the Pygmalion myth, about the sculptor who creates a work of art so beautiful that he falls in love with it, and with Venus’s help, is able to bring his statue to life. In Ovid’s Hellenistic sources, Havelock points out, Pygmalion is a king who orders a statue made of Aphrodite, who then comes to life as herself, not a sculptor who brings to life a maiden through Aphrodite’s intervention (Havelock 130). The complicated mythology surrounding the statue confirms Havelock’s connection of the statue with the Pygmalion myth. Athenaeus writes that the Knidian Aphrodite was modeled on the artist’s lover, Phryne, a famous courte- san who was seen by the artist rising naked from the sea in the manner of Aphrodite herself. At that moment, Praxiteles fell in love with her and soon after, represented her as Aphrodite in his sculpture (11). This myth links the artist, model and work in a closely knit bond of inspira- tion and adoration that is suggestive of the Pygmalion myth. But there was a more ominous aspect to this association as well. According to Pliny the Elder, the statue was so real that “a certain man was once overcome with love for the statue and . . . , after he had hidden himself [in the shrine] during the nighttime, he embraced it and . . . it thus bears a stain, an indication of his lust” (10). The possibility that consumma- tion of sexual desire is capable of “staining” a statue is also raised in the Pygmalion myth, but the story of the Knidian Aphrodite also has other implications. The amorous adventurer here refuses to serve Aph- rodite with due respect and worship, instead demanding that she, a powerful goddess set in her shrine, serve him. This action, tantamount to a symbolic rape, is a treatment of the goddess Aphrodite as if she were the willing courtesan who may have inspired the sculpture. It conceptually transforms the fertility idol from an object of worship, adoration and awe into a vulnerable, helpless representation of human woman, and an object of a degraded masculine lust. It indicates as well the strange correlation between the artist’s model and the artwork it- self. The mythology surrounding the Knidian Aphrodite slides the 308 Critical Insights

sculpture’s identity amidst skillfully sculpted statue, awesome and powerful goddess, sexualized courtesan or violated woman. It thereby complicates the tension between creator and created, life and art, the real and ideal. These are the very tensions revealed in Ovid’s Pygmalion as well. According to Ovid’s Metamorphoses, the famous sculptor Pygmalion is completely repelled by all the women he meets in the real world. Ovid explains that Pygmalion retreats from the prostitutes and other sexually-free women of Amathus, informing us that “Pygmalion knew these women all too well;/ . . ./ He’d better sleep alone.”4 Intimidated by the prospect of woman’s sexual freedom and power, which carry with them the prospect of woman’s own (pro-)creative abilities, Pygmalion fashions a figure that is his, exclusively and completely. He decides to create for himself the ideal woman, a personal possession, in the form of an ivory statue. When it is complete, Pygmalion is over- come by the beauty and perfection of the object he has created: . . . he took to art, Ingenious as he was, and made a creature More beautiful than any girl on earth A miracle of ivory in a statue, So charming that it made him fall in love Her face was life itself. (317-22) Pygmalion, as artist, usurps the power of both (sexual) woman and God in that he creates “life itself,” an artistic child, of sorts. And in fact, he even improves upon both, for the ideal lover he creates for him- self is “More beautiful than any girl on earth.” Important to consider, however, is that Pygmalion is not so much in love with the statue as he is with his own performance and artistry; hence, as we learn that the statue is “yet too modest to permit advances” (323), this is not an indi- cation of the statue’s own “character,” if it can be said to possess one. Refining the Artist into Existence 309

Rather, it is a quality of Pygmalion’s ideal characterization of woman, and he recognizes it as such—viewing this “modesty” as a quality that “showed his art had artful touches in it,/ The kind of art that swept him off his feet” (324-25). And it is precisely the modesty demonstrated in his own “artful” touches that enflames Pygmalion. In refusing sexual activity, his statue implicitly refuses to usurp Pygmalion’s role as cre- ator; her sexual, procreative powers are never a threat to Pygmalion’s artistic creative powers. In other words, Pygmalion’s love for the statue is really narcissism; he loves himself, and in creating art, em- braces his own imaginative, artistic powers of creation.5 Finally, frightened that he might “[stain] that perfect beauty” (Ovid 332) with his impure advances—might transform the statue into the very whore he originally rejected, Pygmalion brings clothing and cov- ers the “modest,” “artful” statue with luxurious silks and jewels, effec- tively cloaking its latent sexuality, and thereby denying the small claim to power it might have been said to possess. But in fact, his love grows so great that Venus takes pity upon him: Then he ran home to see, to touch again The ivory image that his hands contrived, And kissed the sleeping lips, now soft, now warm, Then touched her breasts and cupped them in his hands; They were as though ivory had turned to wax And wax to life, yielding, yet quick with breath . . . He kissed the girl until she woke beneath him Her eyes were shy; she flushed; yet her first look Saw at one glance his face and Heaven above it. (336-80) Pygmalion’s statue becomes a perfect recipient of his desires and a mirror reflection of himself. She has rejected Pygmalion’s advances as a proper and modest woman must do, but she has finally given in, and 310 Critical Insights

“yielded” to his love for her. And as she wakes, she looks up to see Pygmalion and Heaven above him. In her gaze is reflected that which his artful talents have allowed for her to perceive: she understands that Pygmalion must be, to her, the power of perfection, God the Creator; thus his “face and Heaven” meld into one single vision above her. As such, Pygmalion can remain assured of her faithfulness and limited power. Though she is briefly allowed to return his gaze, it is only via his control, and only for the singular purpose of seeing or worshipping Pygmalion as he desires to be seen or worshipped. She has no indepen- dent power; she is an object of contemplation, an idealized mirror of the artist’s desires: a literal extension of him. His love for her is only evidence of his love for himself. It is worth noting that Ovid would have known of the Knidian Aph- rodite and much of the mythology that surrounded the famous sculp- ture. His character’s concern about “staining” the statue, insulting her virtue, relates to the Knidian Aphrodite, that promiscuous goddess of love and fertility, who was already putatively besmirched. Pygmalion’s uncontrollable attraction to his statue is linked to the Knidian Aphro- dite and the sexual and fertility powers she was purported to have pos- sessed. And since the earlier lover is a king, not a sculptor, and the statue is Aphrodite herself, rather than a maiden brought to life by Aphrodite and the artist-lover’s caresses, Ovid’s version dramatizes the power of creation, of artistry, and the artist himself as agent of his creative powers. Thus, it might at first appear that in writing a happy ending to this part of the story—the marriage of Pygmalion and the girl, the true artist who truly brings his art to life—Ovid finds this nar- cissism inherent in their relationship unproblematic, and Pygmalion’s genius as artist something to be lauded, something with which, in fact, the narrator of Metamorphoses seems to identify. On the other hand, Pygmalion’s grandchildren have incestuous relations that offend the gods, which points to Ovid’s disapproval of the couple. It also points to the unnamed girl’s diminished capacity to (pro)create, when compared to Pygmalion, creator of living ideals. In either case Ovid suggests that Refining the Artist into Existence 311

“art” makes man capable of approaching godliness, even allowing him to improve upon God’s work in his success at creating a “living” ideal. But to accept Ovid’s claim that art, here, has become life, means we also accept Ovid’s vision of what life means for a woman: to be alive may be equivalent to being a passive receptacle for male desire, having no will or desire of one’s own, and having no attributes other than per- fect beauty. In short, despite Ovid’s claim that Pygmalion brings movement and warmth to his statue—though he animates her, she does not truly “live.” Though he admires great artistry, Ovid also highlights the audaciousness of Pygmalion’s aspirations, and the transgressive nature of the inanimate statue metamorphosing to life—the same kind of violation of taboo also evident in the mythology surrounding the Knidian Aphrodite. But by the 1900s, centuries of literary, visual, and musical artists had rewritten the story of Pygmalion, and to some degree, tamed it. The Romantics, in particular, idealized the artist’s psychic retreat from society into his or her imagination, and gloried in the sublime artistic creations thereby produced. Because their investigations of Pygmalion entailed an exploration of the metaphysical, they necessarily elided the rigid distinctions between art and life that were so important to Ovid’s version.6 The transcending of these boundaries was continued in Vic- torian and early Modernist works by Oscar Wilde and George Bernard Shaw, for example. In The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890), Wilde re- counts his allegorical tale of an idealized young Narcissus who is the subject of a magical image that ages and mirrors the depravity of his in- creasingly tainted soul: the art almost comes to life while Dorian re- mains in some sense like art, impervious to time and decay. But the moment of transformation, the subject of fervent prayers, sacred ritu- als and deep devotion on the part of Ovid’s Pygmalion, is no more than an offhanded remark by Dorian, in the opening pages of Wilde’s novel. In Shaw’s play Pygmalion (1912), phonetics professor Henry Higgins transforms a flower girl, Eliza Doolittle, into a princess of sorts; by the end, however, the lively Eliza is also transformed by Higgins into an 312 Critical Insights

immobile figure who must conform to society’s expectations in a way that is almost more confining than freeing. But in this case, Shaw uses Pygmalion as a metaphor: unlike Pygmalion’s sculpture, Eliza is never really a statue. I do not mean to suggest that these stories were not radi- cal to their moment, but I do hope to convey that they do not highlight the shocking irreconcilability between art and life with the same force of Ovid’s Pygmalion. James Joyce’s own interest in the Pygmalion theme is evident from his early critical writings on Henrik Ibsen’s When We Dead Awaken (1900),7 a play in which the “matter of life and death [. . . has] implica- tions [that] extend far beyond the ostensible metaphor in the title,”8 but which, like Shaw’s play, uses its relation to the Pygmalion story pri- marily as metaphor. Joyce’s own retelling of the Pygmalion story oc- curs in his 1916 novel, Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. In the re- mainder of this essay, I suggest that unlike Ovid’s Pygmalion, Joyce’s protagonist, Stephen Dedalus, fails to bring art to life because he re- fuses to accept art as anything less than his Romantic concept of per- fection, whereas life is obviously often other than “ideal.” The tradi- tional masculine search for ideals of “Truth” or “Beauty” depicted in Portrait, and epitomized for Stephen in the figure of Saint Thomas Aquinas, is juxtaposed unfavorably with real lived experience—repre- sented by the actual women of the novel, as opposed to those women evoked by Stephen’s imagination. Joyce largely rejects this masculine search for ideals and insists that art requires contribution from this “feminine” side, this real, lived experience, if it is truly to come to life, and if it is truly to emulate this Modernist ideal. Joyce uses Stephen not only to critique Romanticism but, and more importantly for this dis- cussion, to reinvest the Pygmalion story with the impact inherent in Ovid’s transgressive animation of death. Joyce’s protagonist Stephen Dedalus sees himself as conforming to this idealizing artistic tradition in his own development as a writer, de- spite the misogynist implications at work in the Pygmalion story (or perhaps even because of them). If we see Stephen as actually success- Refining the Artist into Existence 313

ful in his “art” by the end of the novel—something I will argue that we should question—the story becomes the equivalent of an artistic bil- dungsroman: the story of how, through trials and tribulations, Stephen Dedalus brings his villanelle to life. In fact, using language and sym- bols directly echoing Ovid’s Pygmalion, Joyce invites us to come to this conclusion.9 Frequently throughout the novel women are de- scribed by Stephen as having “cold,” “ivory” skin, as does the statue. Eileen, for example, has “cool white hands because she was a girl. They were like ivory; only soft,”10 a depiction that correlates Eileen with the Madonna, the great Tower of Ivory (36), in Stephen’s imagina- tion, and yet he insists on an uncharacteristically human “softness” to that ivory, the potential, even in his earliest memories and imagination, for art to come to life. But the analogy between Pygmalion and Portrait extends much fur- ther than language or statuesque women and is particularly related to Stephen’s writing of his villanelle. Like Pygmalion, Stephen rejects the outside world, with its confounding, promiscuous, procreating, and even “whorish” real women, in order to embrace himself as artist. As Archie Loss comments, “Stephen seeks to shelter himself from outer life so that the inner life of the imagination may flourish.”11 In other words, we see Stephen rejecting the real world—“life,” as evidenced in his preparation for work upon the villanelle that culminates his perfor- mance as an artist in Portrait: The full morning light had come. No sound was to be heard: but he knew that all around him life was about to awaken in common noises, hoarse voices, sleepy prayers. Shrinking from that life he turned towards the wall, making a cowl of the blanket and staring at the great overblown scarlet flowers of the tattered wallpaper. (221-22) Referring to this passage, Loss associates Stephen’s “cowl” with a “monkish withdrawal from common life” (Loss 3). Stephen certainly does withdraw from life. But I want to complicate the assumptions we 314 Critical Insights

make regarding gender enough to suggest that though the cowl is monk’s (male) clothing, Stephen may see himself as resembling his lover. For a shawl was also worn like a “cowl” by Emma, the girl at the tram, about whom Stephen’s poem, dedicated to “E. C.,” is ostensibly written (69).12 Stephen writes in Romantic, even Byronic style, elu- sively adopting only Emma’s initials. Then Stephen adorns himself to imitate his lover—a nun, the veiled Madonna; he thus imagines a feminized position, not his own. I will return to Stephen’s recurring habits of feminizing himself later in the course of this essay, but it is significant to note that part of his beloved’s appeal, here, is her imag- ined “monkish” or Madonna-like chastity, her symbolically assured faithfulness to Stephen even as she is assimilated into him. Part of her appeal as well is that in imagining a parallel between Emma and the Madonna, she grants him access to the Madonna’s procreative gift of life everlasting, immortality, the birthing of an ideal—an ability that Stephen both admires and envies. As Suzette Henke comments, “It is not enough to repudiate the female. The artist must usurp her procre- ative powers.”13 Not only does Stephen desire to usurp her creative powers, but in fact, he hopes to improve upon them; like Pygmalion and in emulation of the Madonna, he hopes to create a paradoxical liv- ing perfection. More to the point here is that Stephen not only rejects the outer world’s existence, but he rejects particularly the idea of a shared sexual experience altogether. In person, even his chaste, “cowled” lover would be insufficiently pure for Stephen’s present needs, for this purity assures that Stephen’s lover will not challenge his own creative powers. Like Pygmalion, Stephen knows too well that “he’d better sleep alone.” We should not mistake Stephen’s desire for solitude as a complete, “monkish” or “chaste” denial of his sensual side. Like Pygmalion, in his rejection of the real world, Stephen suddenly finds himself narcis- sistically aroused by the product and beauty of his own imaginative creation: Refining the Artist into Existence 315

A glow of desire kindled again his soul and fired and fulfilled all his body. Conscious of his desire she was waking from odorous sleep, the temptress of his villanelle. Her eyes, dark and with a look of languor, were opening to his eyes. Her nakedness yielded to him, radiant, warm, odorous and lav- ish-limbed, enfolded him like a shining cloud, enfolded him like water with a liquid life: and like a cloud of vapour or like waters circumfluent in space the liquid letters of speech, symbols of the element of mystery, flowed forth over his brain. (223) For Stephen, the act of writing successfully, perhaps both literally and figuratively, results in sexual gratification similar to Pygmalion’s. As Stephen embraces his art, it/she comes to life: first, she becomes “con- scious of his desire,” and therefore, like Pygmalion’s sculpture, wakes from sleep specifically in order to please him. Unlike the audacious real “life” waiting outside the window that is “about to awaken” for anyone and everyone, Stephen opts for a medium which responds only to his own touches and caresses. She begins to be conscious of his gaze, and returns it with “a look of languor,” a kind of submission to Stephen’s poetic and erotic powers. And like the sculpture done by Pygmalion, Stephen’s villanelle “yields” to Stephen as he embraces her, and he feels her come alive beneath his touch. She is now “radiant, warm, odorous and lavish-limbed,” embodied by Stephen’s active art- fulness. In this manner, Stephen is able to “awaken” his sleeping villanelle. Thus far, Stephen’s story could be Pygmalion’s. But some significant distinctions should be noted between the two narratives. Joyce’s narrative contains inverted power dynamics not ev- ident in the original story of Pygmalion, but consistent with Stephen’s fantasies throughout Portrait. Stephen’s art, like Pygmalion’s, remains a narcissistic venture of self-exploration; the woman he imagines is still idealized and a reflection of Stephen’s particular desires. As Charles Rossman observes, E. C. is “a masculine erotic fantasy . . . no more than the self-serving reflection of the man who created her.”14 But Stephen’s poem/lover has the advantage over Pygmalion’s statue 316 Critical Insights

of being capable of a certain kind of sexual action. For Stephen’s lover, though she does “yield” to Stephen’s caresses, also becomes an active lover, who evidences her own desire and Stephen’s comparative passiv- ity by “enfolding” Stephen in her own embrace. Unlike Pygmalion’s statue, which is eventually clothed by Pygmalion to maintain her mod- esty and contain her sexual powers, we discover that, though created from language in the form of a villanelle, Stephen’s lover is a “naked temptress.” Far from the inert, idle statue, Stephen’s fantasy art/woman acts upon him gently, but persistently, “like a shining cloud,” “like waters circumfluent in space.” She represents an intellec- tual, linguistic (as well as sexual) ideal and remains powerful, given that finally, almost through no will of his own, Stephen climaxes, and “language,” in the form of the finally completed villanelle, spills out from his desire: “the liquid letters of speech, symbols of the element of mystery, flowed forth over his brain.” Stephen fantasizes that art or life, in the form of woman, will take him in its grip and wring his pas- sions from him. Paradoxically, Stephen is so terrified of losing control throughout the novel that he can only climax in a situation where he has complete power over his poem/lover. He governs and controls his own feelings and emotions even in the one method open to his narcis- sistic expression: masturbation.15 Oddly, Stephen is considerably more active in his villanelle fantasy than he has been in any of his earlier fantasies and other experiences with real women, which may be evidence of some maturation on his part. For elsewhere, Stephen is marked by his passiveness with women, equally so in his fantasies as he is in reality. In the second chapter, after reading about Mercedes in Alexander Dumas’The Count of Monte Cristo—a Romantic revenge book where the hero controls his passions and ultimately rejects the object of his desires who had once spurned him for another—Stephen fantasizes about meeting the heroine, who would, “without any overt act of his, encounter him” (65). He ironically dreams of life, especially in the form of women, im- posing itself upon him even as he rejects it. And Stephen plays out this Refining the Artist into Existence 317

fantasy of passivity in real life. When he goes in search of a prostitute at the end of the second chapter, for example, he feels himself lured by “a presence subtle and murmurous as a flood filling him wholly with it- self. Its murmur besieged his ears like the murmur of some multitude in sleep; its subtle streams penetrated his being” (100)—an experience which alludes to and prefigures the fantasy-woman of his villanelle. Stephen certainly does not imagine himself as actively searching for carnal knowledge; rather, he sees himself swept along in the dream-like current of something else’s search, waiting to be awakened. In his imagination, it is woman who awakens the sleeping Stephen, and not the reverse. In contrast to Stephen’s listless inertia, women are not merely ac- tive, but so overwhelmingly powerful as to become responsible for creation—at least in Stephen’s mind. “Woman” becomes artist and life collapsed into an ideal image, a mother, a “god,” whose powers are so all-consuming, all-absorbing, that she generates the artist and man that Stephen is to become, reversing the agency of the original Pygmalion. Thus, in his Count of Monte Cristo fantasy, Stephen predicts that “in that moment of supreme tenderness he would be transfigured. He would fade into something impalpable under her eyes and then in a moment, he would be transfigured. Weakness and timidity and inexpe- rience would fall from him in that magic moment” (65). Stephen imag- ines woman molding his mature, masculine shape from his boyish body as if he is clay, “impalpable,” formless, her creative powers paral- leled with her sexual ones, such that an embrace with her causes “weakness” and “timidity” to fall away from him, like articles of un- wanted clothing. This fantasy is realized in a fashion when Stephen embraces the prostitute for the first time at the end of chapter 2. Drawn to the prostitute by some unaccountable phenomenon, Stephen imag- ines himself to be neither directly responsible for the questionable actions of seeking her out, nor for acting in response to her at their first meeting: 318 Critical Insights

His lips would not bend to kiss her. He wanted to be held firmly in her arms, to be caressed slowly, slowly, slowly. In her arms he felt that he had suddenly become strong and fearless and sure of himself. But his lips would not bend to kiss her. With a movement she bowed his head and joined her lips to his and he read the meaning of her movements in her frank uplifted eyes. It was too much for him. He closed his eyes, surrendering himself to her, body and mind, conscious of nothing in the world by the dark pressure of her softly parting lips. They pressed upon his brain as upon his lips as though they were the vehicle of a vague speech. (101) Though Stephen claims that in meeting this woman “he had suddenly become strong and fearless and sure of himself,” he cannot bring him- self to kiss her, and instead, remains passive and “surrendering” to her. He has become the stony, fixed statue that she must move to embrace. The prostitute clearly initiates Stephen into sexual awareness and a certain kind of “experience” of life, but Stephen has not really lost the timidity with women he imagines himself to have lost. He remains in- capable of responding to her dialogue, the physical “vehicle” of expe- rience that becomes a “vague speech” she invites him to share. Their “conversation” remains one-sided; she receives no reply. Real-life ex- perience evidently remains a knowledge that she alone possesses. In- stead, Stephen’s real-life experience is reconsidered until it is no lon- ger real, but rather, corresponds to his earlier fantasy. Instead of searching her out, instead of desiring her for, and by his demands mak- ing her into, the sexually free woman that she is, he becomes the pas- sive receptacle of her desires in his imagination.16 Stephen sees women as responsible for making him into a (young) “man” through his sexual initiation, but he also sees women as making Stephen into an “artist.” Stephen imagines the bird women as the cata- lyst for his becoming an artist, thus imagining woman creating him once more. The way Stephen fantasizes her recalls the moments be- fore, when he had pondered Daedalus, the “fabulous artificer” (169) Refining the Artist into Existence 319

and Stephen’s namesake. Stephen imagines the glory of flying over the ocean with wings of his own making, and then he suddenly happens upon a girl walking along the beach: A girl stood before him in midstream, alone and still, gazing out to sea. She seemed like one whom magic had changed into the likeness of a strange and beautiful seabird. Her long slender bare legs were delicate as a crane’s . . . the white fringes of her drawers were like featherings of soft white down. Her slateblue skirts were kilted boldly about her waist and dove- tailed behind her. Her bosom was as a bird’s soft and slight, slight and soft as the breast of some darkplumaged dove. (171) Stephen sees the girl/bird-woman as a winged symbol of Daedalus, a sign that he is to become the great artificer himself. And in fact, Stephen certainly crafts an “artificial” pair of wings for the object of his desire in transforming her into a bird.17 As he reconfigures her in his imagination, he recognizes his calling to become an “artificer,” which he associates with becoming an “artist.” But as Stephen revisits the event in his mind, it is specifically his encounter with this bird-woman that transforms and “transfigures” him into the artist he wishes to become, rather than the re- verse. As Stephen gazes admiringly at her, “[l]ong, long she suffered his gaze and then quietly withdrew her eyes from his and bent them towards the stream” (171). But Stephen’s reading of this event is that “[h]er eyes had called to him and his soul had leaped at the call. To live, to err, to fall, to triumph, to recreate life out of life!” (172). Again in his reading of this scene, Stephen sees her, and not himself, as the one who initiated con- tact—through speaking to his soul—his own merely responds to hers. And of course in reality, Stephen, as always, remains passive. He stares, is almost invited by her look to speak to her, but he does not, and eventu- ally, she turns away. Far from “living,” or “erring, ” or “falling,” or “tri- umphing,” and even further from “recreat[ing] life out of life,” Stephen does not even respond to a likely invitation from a woman to whom he is attracted. Though he may, as Rossman suggests, recognize the artist’s 320 Critical Insights

duty to translate life and experience into art,18 Stephen fails utterly to embrace life, even when it stares him, literally, in the face. Joyce invites us to suppose that Stephen’s final pride in his own boldness is like that of a silly young child’s, who knows as yet little of living or of life. As both man and artist, Stephen sees himself as “made,” as created by women, not the opposite. By the time Stephen fantasizes about his villanelle, his constant re-ar- ticulation of creative control is commonplace. And though he is, as stated above, more bold with his villanelle than he has been with women—both real and imaginary—previously, the undermining of his initiative is evidenced even in the villanelle. In a fantasy worthy of Leopold Bloom, Stephen at first wakes his villanelle with his desire, but as he rethinks it, he is only responding to the temptation of her naked body. He initiates sex with her yielding body, but ultimately, he imagines that she enfolds him in her embrace instead. And the result, in the villanelle, is a woman who has become the lure of the “fallen seraphim” (223), and the lure of Stephen Dedalus.19 And yet, in his art, as in his imagination, Stephen controls her desires and creative processes—he re- mains her author, even if he envisages himself as somewhat passive. In essence, we can read Stephen as fantasizing woman, who is simulta- neously constructed perfection and powerful creator, both aspects of which are in the end created by him, her author. Like the female creator envied by Stephen and Pygmalion, Stephen aims to create an active, live, sentient but perfect being, of course all the while maintaining con- trol as the artist. This paradox has peculiar implications. It means that Stephen’s real ambitions, far greater than Pygmalion’s, are not merely to “animate,” but rather in some form, to become an author of life; he wants to be a kind of god. In Stephen’s asserting this kind of boldness and con- trol (if only in his artful imagination), it would seem that on some level, conscious or unconscious, Stephen realizes that he must learn to take risks and chances, emotionally and physically, though he is not yet pre- pared to act upon this realization with women in real life. But this “im- provement” is mitigated somewhat by the violence he now enacts upon Refining the Artist into Existence 321

the woman to reduce her power over him even in these fantasies: the fi- nal effect of his fantasized sexual relation with his villanelle is not her embodiment, which might imply her being brought to life, but rather her disembodiment. She becomes “like water with a liquid life: and like a cloud of vapour or like waters circumfluent in space.”20 It would seem that becoming the masculine, active, artistic figure, even within his fan- tasies, is synonymous with doing violence upon the body of woman for Stephen; he must displace the power dynamics he perceives as inherent in woman’s body itself onto himself, thereby dissolving her into noth- ingness, a kind of Pygmalion-like cloaking of her sexuality. Imagining the woman thus, as both his creator and artistic object, has specific advantages for a young man of Stephen’s temperament. If Ste- phen’s artwork is any less than perfect, the fault is not his, but lies with the beloved of Stephen’s poem, who lures him into adoration and ser- vice, and away from his art. Indeed the bird woman brazenly, wantonly demands him with her eyes, her soul, and Stephen resists her charms in order to take on such impulsive challenges as becoming an artist. In Ste- phen’s imagination, if his villanelle is a failure, if it is somehow less than ideal, “pure,” perfection, it is because its muse, its inspiration, is also less than pure. Thus the heavenly “wild angel” is quickly transformed into the greatest seducer of all time, the “lure of the fallen seraphim,” the lit- eral “villan/elle,” the feminine villain of Stephen’s story. But unlike Pygmalion, Stephen is destined to fail, victim to his evil temptress, which is really nothing more than the wicked betrayal of his own idealizing tendencies; he never reaches the epiphany that Gabriel Conroy achieves at the end of “The Dead,” when he realizes, not unkindly, that his idealized and idolized wife is no longer beautiful. Ste- phen’s dehumanizing, idealizing tendency is the only “woman” who stops him from living more fully, and embracing life’s imperfections and wonders. In reality, if the villanelle is a failure—and it is a failure—the fault lies with Stephen, who projects the trite fantasy of the ideal woman into his villanelle. He has indeed become something like the great Daedalus in that he is a “fabulous artificer,” but his skills are limited to 322 Critical Insights

the “artificial” and “unreal” precisely because Stephen remains unin- formed by experience. The bird-woman is not a tantalizing seductress, nor is she an ardent angel, nor is she some ideal sexualized combination of the two; she is merely a girl who, with her gaze, invites Stephen to speak to her. When he does not, she turns away. Everything else Stephen sees is a figment of his (over)active imagination, which constantly re- jects the real world in favor of a preferred aesthetic ideal. In concrete terms, woman does not create Stephen as either artist or man. If Stephen can be said to have been “created” by anything, it is his environment. Henke describes Stephen’s surroundings as “Mother Church and Mother Ireland,”21 but I find them to be more related to the extremely patriarchal structure of his all-male religious and educational back- ground, represented in the figure of Saint Thomas Aquinas.22 In a recent essay, Ian Crump insists that Stephen’s theory of excel- lent (aesthetic) writing calls for an extraordinarily controlled project, designed for the artist to eventually initiate his own complete absence from his work of art. In this effort, the artist’s work becomes a modi- fied version of Aquinas’s spiritual “Truth”: an ideal “Beauty.” Crump succinctly explains the theory Stephen espouses: Stephen asserts, in a passage which first appeared in the final version of the theory, that, as the artist progresses through the three forms [lyrical, ep- ochal and dramatic], his personality becomes increasingly impersonal in, or absent from, the aesthetic image that he presents in increasingly imme- diate relation to ‘the indifferent public.’ 23 Stephen likes to imagine himself as even more powerful and God-like than Pygmalion, who needed the seductive arts of Venus to awaken his faithful lover. Stephen makes himself into the autonomous creator of perfect beauty: he would like to imagine himself impersonally assert- ing control, objectively downplaying the role of his personality in the artwork; he would like to imagine himself as an authoritative man, who crafts “Truth” and “Beauty” so subconsciously that it is almost effort- Refining the Artist into Existence 323

less. Stephen’s aspiration is to become the ideal artist of his dreams, where the “artist, like the God of the creation, remains within or behind or beyond or above his handiwork, invisible, refined out of existence, indifferent, paring his fingernails” (215). In search of the ideal artist, Joyce connects Stephen not only with Pygmalion, but to Praxiteles and the mythology of the Knidian Aphro- dite. In a conversation with Lynch, Stephen insists that art must inspire only the most pure and sublime reactions in its viewers. But Lynch is al- ways degrading the esoteric level of their conversations by bringing the vulgar element of life back into them. He comments, “You say that art must not excite desire . . . I told you that one day I wrote my name in pen- cil on the backside of Venus of Praxiteles in the Museum. Was that not desire?” (205). Stephen disregards Lynch’s comment, stating offhand- edly, “I speak of normal natures” (205). But in fact, Lynch speaks di- rectly to the heart of the problem. He asks if writing one’s name on the back of Praxiteles’s Venus, the Knidian Aphrodite, bespeaks desire. Like the legendary lover of ancient times, Lynch has consummated his “desire” with a stain upon the statue. Stephen ironically rejects Lynch’s expression of desire, suggesting that his “flesh responded to the stimulus of a naked statue” (206). In this case, however, Stephen seems to will- fully misread the incident, for Lynch’s desire is articulated in written form, rather than sexual. Even when Lynch leeringly observes that the hypotenuse of a right triangle is much less attractive than the hypotenuse of Praxiteles’s Venus, his response, graffiti, is actually far more detached than Stephen realizes, and far more detached, of course, than Stephen himself is in practice with his own art. Lynch signs his name, almost act- ing out Stephen’s secret desires in a sniggering kind of authorial posses- sion of the naked statue, claiming the right of a creator to the creative powers inherent in a sexually active woman and fertility goddess. As with the lover of the Knidian Aphrodite, Lynch does not serve the god- dess with his prayers and respectful adoration, but instead seeks to con- trol and possess her powers in a vulgar expression of irreverence. For all that Stephen insists that detachment is essential for artistic, 324 Critical Insights

aesthetic creation, and for all that he accuses Lynch of failing to be de- tached in his appreciation of the Knidian Aphrodite, it is Stephen who fails to remain detached; it is Stephen who physically desires statu- esque women. Unlike Lynch, Stephen wants his authorial possession to be marked not only in linguistic terms, but in sexual ones, like the Knidian Aphrodite’s mythical molester. As such, the Knidian Aphro- dite is a disconcerting example because it represents, like the ivory vir- gin mother, a statuesque conflation of impossible feminine ideals that becomes the paradoxical metonymy for Stephen of all women. De- pending slightly on the copy to which Stephen and Lynch refer, the na- ked statue is posed so that her right hand ambivalently both covers and points to her pudendum (Havelock 36)24 or “aidos” in Greek, which means “modesty,” “shame,” and “awe” (Havelock 28),25 a title which bears uncanny resemblance to Stephen’s understanding of reproduc- tive woman, who possessed “the strange humiliation of her nature” (222).26 The statue’s exact pose is debated: is it designed to represent the goddess emerging from her bath where she is caught, unaware, by voyeurs, and covers her body, her “shame,” out of “modesty” like a vulnerable woman might do?, or does her right hand point to her pu- dendum in a proud, goddess-like indexing of the exact source of her powers of fertility and abilities to inspire desire in the male viewer?27 Thus the Knidian Aphrodite manifests a conflation of the kind of the mutually exclusive ideals Stephen projects onto all the women of the novel: she is paradoxically promiscuous but virginal, powerful but vulnerable, creator and creation. This figure, to which Lynch unprob- lematically and playfully lays claim, represents everything that Ste- phen both adamantly admires and is threatened by in woman. But in Stephen’s case, he not only wants to possess it with a written signature of ownership, he also wants to possess it sexually, to father, like Pygmalion, a living ideal. Lynch’s phallic pencil stain on the Knidian Aphrodite foreshadows the more symbolic, sexual stain Stephen will leave on the temptress of his villanelle, “an indication of his lust,” and a suggestion that he will debase the extraordinary powers of Venus, of Refining the Artist into Existence 325

true love, in exchange for masculine sexual possession. Stephen’s downfall in the villanelle is his obsession with traditional masculine ideals. His problem is that he waits for a world that con- forms to the ideals of his preferred male philosophers. For Aquinas the ideal woman is the rational impossibility represented in the Tower of Ivory, the Virgin Mary, the Venus of Praxiteles. When, as it must, the real world fails to conform to these ideals, Stephen hides in his own in- terior world where he can still continue to hold onto his ideals, modi- fied from Aquinas’. The ardent “temptress” of his poem, the woman alluring enough to tempt Satan himself, with “languorous look and lavish limb!” is not real, but ideal; one might claim she is even cliché. While his villanelle is technically correct, as Stephen’s imaginary critic, Emma’s priest-uncle concludes (222),28 indeed it is among the more difficult and controlled forms of poetry to write, it is precisely Stephen’s distance from the experience of the “real,” the experience of “life” that prevents him from becoming the artist he aspires to become. As Rossman puts it, Stephen “cannot become an ‘artist’ without a pre- requisite metamorphosis of character which puts an end to the alien- ation that the poem reveals” (282). Stephen consistently replaces his extreme fantasies of the “Virgin” and “whore” with some conflation of the two in order to find space between them and create a new, but still idealized beloved. Yet he has only to open his eyes to the women who care for him—the women Cranly immediately understands, in order to see all the possibilities that lie between the two extremes. As Albert Wachtel suggests, “Stephen distorts his subjects for the sake of what he fancies to be beautiful.”29 Rather than recognizing that his personal, unique experiences and thoughts are what make his art (and women) truthful and beautiful, Stephen is bent on controlling and conforming his imaginary life to traditional absolutes and ideals of “Truth” and “Beauty,” in the manner of a masculine tradition—in the manner of Pygmalion. Herein lies his failure: Stephen writes from the experience of others, imitating Byron and other favorite artists, instead of from his own experience. And as David Wright comments, “we detect Joyce’s 326 Critical Insights

own conviction that artistic precepts—and hence practice—cannot be divorced from experience.”30 Stephen cannot yet love real woman, and so his art cannot reflect the love that is necessary to bring his poetry to life. He uses art to shield him from experience, absenting himself from experience, instead of using lived experience to inspire his art. Ultimately, Ian Crump asserts that not only Stephen, but Joyce as well buys into the theory of aesthetic masculinized absenting of the art- ist from the object of the art (Crump 223). He argues that Joyce works to absent himself from his art, and proposes this as an ideal. But to sug- gest that Joyce subscribes to Stephen’s theory is to ignore not only the use Joyce makes of autobiographical details but also the ironic dis- tance that Joyce creates from his hero, as Stephen becomes more ar- rogant and less invested—even “disinterested”—with real life. As Joseph Buttigieg agrees, the “‘disinterested’ critics are serving an ob- vious self-interest when they appropriate Stephen Dedalus’s aesthetic theory and invest it with an authority which is not furnished by the text itself.”31 I would agree with Rossman, Buttigieg and Wright, and argue that the real “authority” of Joyce’s text gives primacy not to “male” ideals, but to a “female” experience of life, as exemplified in the con- trasting description between Joyce’s male and female characters. Whereas the men of Portrait often demand a tempering of emotion, of expression, of “life,” the women of the story seem to embrace their ex- periences fully and freely. Stephen and other men read emotions pejo- ratively, as with his mother: “She was a nice mother but she was not so nice when she cried” (9). Dante, passionately angry, cannot finish Christmas dinner with the Dedalus family (39). By contrast, though Stephen is angry on one occasion, he believes that “his anger lent noth- ing to the vision [of squalor and insincerity reshaping the world about him]. He chronicled with patience what he saw, detaching himself from it” (67). Even from an early age, Stephen distances himself from his feelings, denying his emotional side in favor of detachment not possessed by the women of the novel. Certainly, Stephen’s youthful misogyny is derived in part from this repression of expression. In his Refining the Artist into Existence 327

emulation of this masculine tradition, Stephen forgets that his old fa- ther Daedalus’ son, Icarus, is destined to take a very nasty fall. Perhaps Stephen recognizes the failure of his poem in the final pages of the novel, for the comments in his diary suggest how troubled he has become by any suggestion of woman’s sexuality, which does successfully recreate life from life. He resents and rejects any repre- sentation of this sexuality, even dormant in woman’s inert artistic body: “Statues of women,” he speculates thinking back to his con- versation with Lynch, “should always be fully draped” (251). The Knidian Aphrodite, which had once seemed vulnerable and able to be possessed, Stephen now sees as threatening him, glorying in a power that she possesses and he does not. Woman’s seductive, reproductive power must be cloaked and, like Pygmalion’s statue, Stephen wants to see her covered by the end of the book. Stephen’s frustration becomes evident in his real life as well. He becomes increasingly isolated and passive, rejecting religion, Ireland, and family. He finally rejects his real-life beloved because he judges her (unfairly) like all other women, as unfaithful to him for “flirting” with her “priest” (216). Powerful women in Stephen’s fantasy life are an indication of their (unknowing) power over him in reality, which inspires such ridiculous interpreta- tions of even the most innocent gestures, such as seeing his beloved’s intimacy with her confessor as erotic.32 Joyce does not condone Portrait’s men’s total repression of life. He smiles upon the awkward Emma, who “comes up to his [Stephen’s] step many times . . . urg[ing] her vanities, . . . asking him would he take her gift to which he had only to stretch out his hand . . . [to] hold her and kiss her” (70); he derisively mocks the cowardly Stephen who, though he desires her, refuses her, and even later, only expresses his love by leaving “foul long letters . . . of guilty confession . . . only to throw them under the cover of night . . . where a girl might come upon them as she walked by and read them secretly” (116). Whereas the cold school and churches are gendered masculine by the very patriarchal nature of institutions and their all-male populations, the city itself, characterized 328 Critical Insights

not only by whores, but also hustle and bustle, business, movement, and “life” in general, is naturalized and feminized: “The rain had drawn off; and amid the moving vapours from point to point of light the city was spinning about herself a soft cocoon of yellowish haze” (138). Stephen’s “old father” of the novel’s last few lines, an appella- tion indicating both his real father and Daedalus of the classic mascu- line tradition which has raised him in its likeness, is, like Stephen, an “old artificer” (253). Simon Dedalus is content, even proud, to see his son raised in a masculine tradition, unquestioning of the ideas which have formed him, oblivious to the richness that real life—in the form of his wife and children—offers him. This masculine tradition, as evi- denced from Simon Dedalus’s anatomy classroom in Cork, produces nothing more than an unborn, unbirthed, even symbolic child, repre- sented in the word “Foetus,” cut into the desk of the classroom (89). This word horrifies Stephen in that it reminds him, as Michael H. Begnal points out, of his own “immature state” (Begnal 107), but it also functions as a harbinger of Stephen’s father’s intellectual tradition, his father’s inability to “recreate life from life.” In contrast, Stephen’s mother, whom Stephen sees as having had so little influence upon her son, understands real creation, and therefore knows what Stephen, the boy, must do to become both an artist and a man: she prays “that [Stephen] may learn in [his] own life and away from home and friends what the heart is and what it feels” (252). This service to love, and to life, which Stephen “will not serve” (246), is what his mother hopes he will learn elsewhere. Her hopes may have begun to be realized in Stephen’s surprised and uncharacteristically non-idealizing description of his beloved in the final pages of his diary, where he admits, “Yes, I liked her today. Alittle or much? Don’t know. I liked her and it seems a new feeling to me” (252). But his mother’s hopes also hint at her recognition that not only has Stephen tried to conform the women to his ideals, but he has also struggled to live up to an impossible masculine ideal himself. What Stephen recognizes and grapples with throughout this novel is not only his own lack of control Refining the Artist into Existence 329

over the feminine influences of his life, but also over the lack of control of the “feminine” sides of himself. In this sense, Stephen’s becoming both an artist and man are intricately tied to “femininity” and “femi- nine” creativity; this nurturing acceptance of real experience, denial of idealizations, gives the women characters an advantage over their male counterparts in understanding and reading real “life” for Joyce. This “femininity” has an advantage that Stephen has heretofore ignored. Joyce creates Stephen in such a way that he truly possesses a femi- nine side of himself, his consciousness. The fact that Stephen aligns himself with his lover’s perspectives instead of his own sets the ground for the potential in Stephen to tap into his feminine soul, and into the feminine creative ability in his conscious and real experience of life as inspiration in his art. Furthermore, Stephen is far more personally in- volved in the composition of his villanelle than he ever admits to his friend, Lynch, or than he explains using his grandiose “aesthetic the- ory.” As Begnal comments, “despite all of Stephen’s pontificating about art and beauty, he is much better at kinetic beauty than he is at the static” (Begnal 114). Stephen’s reaction to his art is far less “objective” and “outside” than he likes to imagine it. Certainly Stephen is occupied in a much more productive and personal manner than “indifferent par- ing [of] his fingernails” when he dexterously composes his “hand/work.” The writing literally becomes an “intimate” experience for him, with all the qualities of fantasy. Like Pygmalion, Stephen’s writing reflects his desires; it cannot be separated from him, is an ex- tension of him. Though Joyce disapproves of Stephen’s alienation of reality and his idealization of the world, Joyce is not critical of Ste- phen’s intimacy with his work. This burgeoning of an intimate and per- sonal experience with his art leaves room for hope of Stephen’s suc- cess as an artist. In this sense, Stephen’s impulses are correct; the ideals of “Beauty” or “Truth” cannot be located from an objective “outside” position because they do not exist. In searching the realm of the per- sonal, the intimate—even the traditionally coded “feminine” spaces, Stephen implicitly makes room for the possibility of the Modernist re- 330 Critical Insights

fusal of the ideal in favor of new visions of “truths” and “beauties.” This insight and ability is what gives young Stephen Dedalus the po- tential to become a great artist. To do so, however, requires that, in a habit unfamiliar to Pygmalion, Stephen must sometimes live outside of his studio, outside of his imagination. Whether James Joyce himself accomplishes the standards and char- acter of art that I claim he espouses in Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man is debatable. He clearly draws from real-life experience, as Ste- phen Dedalus is largely autobiographical. His “stream of conscious- ness” style is another method of collapsing the distinctions of “art” versus “life.” In fact, Wright goes so far as to suggest that, as with Ste- phen’s villanelle, there is “a sense in which Stephen, as a character who is not Joyce, ‘creates’the novel—in that it only exists as a record of the distinct individual, Stephen Dedalus and his responses to experience” (39). But for all his conscious embrace of the “feminine” experience of real life, Joyce carefully controls his final product through his gram- matical distance; it is a finely tuned, highly wrought work—one that asserts his expertise in the masculine tradition of writing as well. As Ian Crump insists, “Joyce hoped to intellectualize himself by gram- matically distancing his present self from his past selves: he writes of them in the third person and uses passive constructions and indistinct assertions” (231). Portrait is evidence that Joyce, like his sometimes autobiographical protagonist Stephen Dedalus, continued to struggle with incorporating real world experiences, love, and his “feminine” side, into his writing. But the struggle in and of itself dramatizes Joyce’s deep understanding of the conflict so critical to Ovid’s story: the real violation of the taboo involved in translating art into life. He writes “Emma is implicated in Stephen’s sinfulness: he has his Blessed Virgin equate them by saying, ‘You have erred but you are always my chil- dren’(P 116), a gratuitous sharing with Emma of his adventures in the brothels” (36). 17. In his reading of the bird woman scene, Begnal treats Stephen’s vision of the girl as an artistic endeavor itself, critically asserting, for example, “Her long fair hair is ‘girlish,’an adjective that makes little specific, visual sense. What is ‘girlish’hair? . . . [The bird woman’s] image will ultimately send Stephen off to sleep, as it just might af- fect a reader. . . . Its language lacks precision. What Stephen sees as a transformative moment in his path of life, Begnal sees as inauspicious and riddled with problems from the outset. 18. Now, he suddenly makes a Nietzschean commitment to the earth and the values of the body—to the ‘fair courts of life.’ Furthermore, his new commitment implies an artistic mandate: Art can no longer substitute for experience by vicariously gratifying life’s frustrated yearn- ings. Now, art will build on experience—the poet will ‘recreate life out of life’” (283). Though he will use Stephen’s scene with his beloved, Rossman too suggests that “Ste- phen is still as alienated from her, still as incapable of effective action, as he had been ten years before on the steps of the tram. In Portrait] Emma has now lost her sur- name, and except for a single incident when Stephen imagines a marriage in heaven performed by the Blessed Virgin (P 115-16), where ‘Emma’ is used three times, even her Christian name is absent. Chronology of James Joyce’s Life and Times 1882 James Augustine Aloysius Joyce is born on February 2. Adeline Virginia Woolf is born on January 25. Eamon de Valera is born on October 14. Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Henry Burke are murdered in Phoenix Park, Dublin. John O’Leary and Douglas Hyde found the Irish National Literary Society. Charles Robert Darwin dies on April 19. Electrical Age begins. 1883 Franz Kafka is born. Karl Heinrich Marx dies. 1884 The first edition of Oxford English Dictionary is published. The Berlin Conference and the European “scramble for Africa.” Michael Cusack founds the Gaelic Athletic Association. 1885 Ezra Pound is born. 1886 Emily Dickinson dies. Charles Stewart Parnell and William Ewart Gladstone’s Irish Home Rule Bill is defeated. Karl Friedrich Benz patents a gasoline-powered motor vehicle. 1887 Bloody Sunday. 1888 Joyce enrolls in Clongowes Wood College. Thomas Sterns Eliot is born. William Butler Yeats founds the Pan-Celtic Society. George Eastman patents the Kodak Camera. 1889 Yeats publishes The Wanderings of Oisin. Gerard Manley Hopkins dies. Parnell and Katherine O’Shea are involved in scandal. Paris Exposition. The Eiffel Tower is built as the entrance to the World’s Fair. Chronology 337

1891 Arthur Rimbaud dies. George Bernard Shaw publishes The Quintessence of Ibsenism. Parnell marries O’Shea on June 25; he dies on October 6. 1892 Walt Whitman dies. 1893 Joyce enrolls in Belvedere College. The Gaelic League is founded. A second Home Rule Bill is rejected by the British House of Lords. Chicago World’s Fair features Nicola Tesla’s alternating current lights and Thomas Edison’s incandescent bulbs. George Ferris’s wheel spins freight trains. Skyscrapers are built on floating foundations. Henry Ford manufactures his first car. 1895 Oscar Wilde is arrested for “gross indecency.” X rays are discovered by Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen. 1896 Paul Verlaine dies. The first electric tram begins operating in Dublin. The first cinema shows appear in Dublin. 1898 Stéphane Mallarmé dies. Gladstone dies. Irish Local Government Act. 1899 Joyce enrolls in University College, Dublin. Yeats publishes The Wind Among the Reeds; his play The Countess Cathleen is produced. United Irishman newspaper is founded. Second Boer War begins. Sigmund Freud publishes Interpretation of Dreams. 1900 A review of Henrik Ibsen’s “New Drama” is published in Fortnightly Review. Wilde dies. Max Planck invents quantum physics. 338 Critical Insights

1901 Joyce publishes “The Day of the Rabblement.” Queen Victoria dies and is succeeded by Edward VII. Hyde’s play The Twisting of the Rope is produced (performed in Irish). The first Nobel Prizes are awarded. 1903 Joyce begins composing Stephen Hero. The Wright brothers’ achieve flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. 1904 Joyce writes “A Portrait of an Artist.” Early Dubliners stories are published in the Fortnightly Review. Joyce elopes with Nora Barnacle to Pola, Austria-Hungary. The Abbey Theatre opens. 1905 Joyce’s son Giorgio is born. Arthur Griffith founds Sinn Féin. Albert Einstein publishes his “Miracle Year” papers on the photoelec- tric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and the equivalence of matter and energy. 1906 Joyce lives briefly in Rome, Italy; tries to get early version of Dubliners published. Ibsen dies. Samuel Beckett is born. Michael Davitt dies. 1907 Joyce returns to Trieste, Italy. Chamber Music is published. Joyce’s daughter Lucia is born. Joyce begins transforming Stephen Hero into A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. He writes “The Dead” and also publishes political essays about Ire- land in Trieste newspapers. He publishes “Ireland, Island of Saints and Sages.” Rudyard Kipling wins the Nobel Prize in Literature. John Millington Synge’s play The Playboy of the Western World is produced. 1908 A 40,000-year-old Neanderthal skeleton is found in France. Chronology 339

1909 Joyce ventures on a business trip to Dublin. Synge dies. Filippo Tommaso Marinetti publishes his “Futurist Manifesto.” 1910 Joyce tries to get an enlarged version of Dubliners published; he pub- lishes the article “The Home Rule Comet.” Mark Twain dies. George V becomes king of the United Kingdom. William James dies. Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell publish their Principia Mathematica. 1911 Joyce lectures on Shakespeare in Trieste. Kasimir Edschmid publishes “On Literary Expressionism.” The British House of Lords is denied ultimate veto. 1912 Joyce makes his final business trip to Dublin; he publishes “The Shade of Parnell” The third Home Rule Bill passes; it is later postponed due to World War I. 1914 Dubliners is published. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man is serialized in The Egoist. World War I begins (1914-1918). 1915 Joyce begins working on Ulysses and Exiles in Zurich, Switzerland. Einstein presents his theory of general relativity. 1916 A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man is published in the United States. Henry James dies. Hugo Ball publishes his “Dada Manifesto.” Easter Rising. More than one million soldiers die during the Battle of the Somme in France. 1917 A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man is published in England. 1918 Ulysses is serialized in the Little Review. Tristan Tzara et al. publish their “Dada Manifesto.” 340 Critical Insights

1919 The Irish Parliament, Dáil Éireann, is established, and de Valera is elected its president. Irish War of Independence. Einstein’s theory of general relativity is confirmed by Arthur Edding- ton’s observation of the total solar eclipse of May 29. 1920 Upon invitation from Ezra Pound, Joyce heads to Paris, France. A U.S. court halts the serializing of Ulysses as obscene. Bloody Sunday in Croagh Park. 1921 The Irish Free State is established. The province of Northern Ireland is established in the United King- dom. Einstein receives the Nobel Prize in Physics. 1922 Sylvia Beach publishes Ulysses in Paris, France. T. S. Eliot publishes The Waste Land. Irish Civil War begins. Michael Collins is killed. 1923 Yeats recieves the Nobel Prize in Literature. 1924 Transatlantic Review begins publishing Work in Progress (later retitled Finnegans Wake). Shaw’s play Saint Joan is published. Irish Civil War ends. 1925 Kafka publishes The Trial. F. Scott Fitzgerald publishes The Great Gatsby. Shaw wins the Nobel Prize in Literature. 1926 Rainer Maria Rilke dies. Ernest Hemingway publishes The Sun Also Rises. 1927 Pomes Penyeach is published. Woolf publishes To the Lighthouse. The Jazz Singer, the first “talkie” film, is released. 1928 Thomas Hardy dies. Chronology 341

1929 William Faulkner publishes The Sound and the Fury. The Great Depression begins. 1930 Pluto is discovered. 1932 De Valera becomes prime minister of Ireland. 1934 Ulysses is published in the United States. 1936 Ulysses is published in England. 1939 Finnegans Wake is published. Joyce moves back to Zurich. Yeats dies. World War II begins (1939-1945). Freud dies. 1941 Joyce dies on January 13; he is buried in Zurich. Woolf dies on March 28. The Manhattan Project is approved. 342 Critical Insights

About the Editor Albert Wachtel is Professor of Creative Studies and English at Claremont’s Pitzer College and the Claremont Graduate University. He is the author of The Cracked Lookingglass: James Joyce and the Nightmare of History (1992) and coeditor of Mod- ernism: Challenges and Perspectives (1986). A National Defense Education Act and Creative Arts Institute Fellow and Danforth Associate, he has published criticism ranging from ancient Greek tragedy, for which he received grants from the National Endowment for the Humanities, to contemporary events; he writes fiction and drama and brings the perspective of a creative writer to bear on his critical explorations. His stories and articles have appeared in journals, magazines, and newspapers, including The Gettysburg Review, Grove, James Joyce Quarterly, the Los Angeles Examiner, the Los Angeles Times, Midstream, Moment Magazine, the San Francisco Chronicle, the Southern Review, Spectrum, and the Wall Street Journal. His adaptation of Shake- speare’s Henry IV, Part 1 and Part 2, was performed at the Odyssey Theater. He has written many essays for Salem Press’s Masterplots and has lectured nationally and in- ternationally on modernism and Joyce’s fiction. About The Paris Review The Paris Review is America’s preeminent literary quarterly, dedicated to discov- ering and publishing the best new voices in fiction, nonfiction, and poetry. The maga- zine was founded in Paris in 1953 by the young American writers Peter Matthiessen and Doc Humes, and edited there and in New York for its first fifty years by George Plimpton. Over the decades, the Review has introduced readers to the earliest writings of Jack Kerouac, Philip Roth, T. C. Boyle, V. S. Naipaul, Ha Jin, Ann Patchett, Jay McInerney, Mona Simpson, and Edward P. Jones, and published numerous now- classic works, including Roth’s Goodbye, Columbus, Donald Barthelme’s Alice, Jim Carroll’s Basketball Diaries, and selections from Samuel Beckett’s Molloy (his first publication in English). The first chapter of Jeffrey Eugenides’s The Virgin Suicides appeared in the Review’s pages, as have stories by Rick Moody, David Foster Wallace, Denis Johnson, Jim Crace, Lorrie Moore, and Jeanette Winterson. The Paris Review’s renowned Writers at Work series of interviews, whose early in- stallments include legendary conversations with E. M. Forster, William Faulkner, and Ernest Hemingway, is one of the landmarks of world literature. The interviews re- ceived a George Polk Award and were nominated for a Pulitzer Prize. Among the more than three hundred interviewees are Robert Frost, Marianne Moore, W. H. Auden, Elizabeth Bishop, Susan Sontag, and Toni Morrison. Recent issues feature conversa- tions with Jonathan Franzen, Norman Rush, Louise Erdrich, Joan Didion, Norman Mailer, R. Crumb, Michel Houellebecq, Marilynne Robinson, David Mitchell, Annie About the Editor 351

Proulx, and Gay Talese. In November 2009, Picador published the final volume of a four-volume series of anthologies of Paris Review interviews. The New York Times called the Writers at Work series “the most remarkable and extensive interviewing project we possess.” The Paris Review is edited by Lorin Stein, who was named to the post in 2010. The editorial team has published fiction by Lydia Davis, André Aciman, Sam Lipsyte, Damon Galgut, Mohsin Hamid, Uzodinma Iweala, James Lasdun, Padgett Powell, Richard Price, and Sam Shepard. Recent poetry selections include work by Frederick Seidel, Carol Muske-Dukes, John Ashbery, Kay Ryan, Mary Jo Bang, Sharon Olds, Charles Wright, and Mary Karr. Writing published in the magazine has been antholo- gized in Best American Short Stories (2006, 2007, and 2008), Best American Poetry, Best Creative Non-Fiction, the Pushcart Prize anthology, and O. Henry Prize Stories. The magazine presents three annual awards. The Hadada Award for lifelong contri- bution to literature has recently been given to Joan Didion, Norman Mailer, Peter Matthiessen, John Ashbery, and, in 2010, Philip Roth. The Plimpton Prize for Fiction, awarded to a debut or emerging writer brought to national attention in the pages of The Paris Review, was presented in 2007 to Benjamin Percy, to Jesse Ball in 2008, and to Alistair Morgan in 2009. In 2011, the magazine inaugurated the Terry Southern Prize for Humor. The Paris Review was a finalist for the 2008 and 2009 National Magazine Awards in fiction and won the 2007 National Magazine Award in photojournalism. The Los Angeles Times recently called The Paris Review “an American treasure with true inter- national reach,” and the New York Times designated it “a thing of sober beauty.” Since 1999 The Paris Review has been published by The Paris Review Foundation, Inc., a not-for-profit 501(c)(3) organization. Contributors Albert Wachtel is Professor of Creative Studies and English at Pitzer College and the Claremont Graduate University. He is the author of The Cracked Lookingglass: James Joyce and the Nightmare of History and coeditor of Modernism: Challenges and Perspectives. His stories and articles have appeared in The Gettysburg Review, the James Joyce Quarterly, the Los Angeles Times, the San Francisco Chronicle, the Southern Review, the Wall Street Journal, and other publications. Tara Prescott received her Ph.D. in English, specializing in twentieth-century American literature, from Claremont Graduate University. Her dissertation, “A ‘Lyric Elixir’: The Search for Identity in the Works of Mina Loy,” includes a chapter on the connections between James Joyce and Mina Loy. Her recent publications have been featured in European Joyce Studies and Women’s Studies. Patrick Loughran is a writer and editor based in London. His work has appeared in The Times of London, the Irish News, and Al Majalla, and on the Paris Review Daily. He is from Belfast. Melissa Free, a Visiting Assistant Professor at Binghamton University, State Uni- versity of New York, teaches nineteenth- and twentieth-century British literature and postcolonial studies. Her work has appeared in Joyce Studies Annual, Studies in the Novel, Texas Studies in Literature and Language, Book History, and The Social Con- text of Freakery in Britain, edited by Marlene Tromp. Her book project, “‘That Inde- finable Something Besides’: Southern Africa, British Identity, and the Authorial Infor- mant,” examines the role of southern Africa in the constitution of British identity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Maureen O’Connor teaches English at the National University of Ireland, Galway. She is the author of The Female and the Species: The Animal in Irish Women’s Writing (2010), editor of Back to the Future of Irish Studies: Festschrift for Tadhg Foley (2010), and coeditor, with Tadhg Foley, of Ireland and India: Colonies, Culture, and Empire (2006); with Kathryn Laing and Sinéad Mooney, of Edna O’Brien: New Criti- cal Perspectives (2006); and with Lisa Colletta, of Wild Colonial Girl: Essays on Edna O’Brien (2006). Parker Douglas received his Ph.D. in English from the University of California, Santa Barbara, and his J.D. from the University of Utah, where he edited the Utah Law Review. Trained in literary theory, he has previously written and published articles on literature, history, constitutional law, and philosophy, as well as media studies and contemporary fiction. He is currently Assistant Federal Defender for the District of Utah and spends some of his time reading and speaking about the work and life of James Joyce. Hugh Kenner, one of the fountainheads of scholarship on modernism, was Profes- sor of English at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Johns Hopkins Univer- Contributors 353

sity, and the University of Georgia; he died in 2003. Of his collection of outstanding books on the modernists, his first on Joyce, Dublin’s Joyce (1956, 1987), was a crucial source for the vast network of studies that followed. The Pound Era (1971) is gener- ally regarded as his most comprehensive work. Richard M. Kain, formerly Professor and Chairman of the Humanities Division at the University of Louisville, was lost to the world of Joyce scholarship in 1990. Of his many important contributions, the landmark Fabulous Voyager: James Joyce’s “Ulys- ses” (1947) was his first book. Perhaps the most useful for research on Joyce’s Portrait is primary source material he coedited, The Workshop of Daedalus: James Joyce and the Raw Materials for “A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man” (1965). Marian Eide is Associate Professor of English at Texas A&M University. She is the author of Ethical Joyce (2002, 2008) and several articles on modernism. She is cur- rently working on a study of violence in twentieth-century aesthetics. John W. Mahon is Professor of English at Iona College. He edits and writes from an engaged perspective on Irish literature and Shakespeare. Iona College was founded by the Christian Brothers, for whom Professor Mahon’s loyalty and respect are evident. Edmund L. Epstein, Professor of English at Queens College and the Graduate Cen- ter of City University, New York, has been a major voice of Joyce criticism for more than half a century. His most recent book is A Guide Through “Finnegans Wake” (2009). Jonathan Mulrooney, Associate Professor of English at the College of the Holy Cross, writes on Irish literature, Romanticism, theater, and film. He is currently work- ing on a book with the working title Keats’s Disappearing Figures. Tracey Teets Schwarze, formerly Professor of English and Vice Provost of Chris- topher Newport University, died in the midst of her career in August 2010. She wrote Joyce and the Victorians (2002). Bonnie Roos is Assistant Professor of English at West Texas A&M University. Her publications include “Joyce’s ‘The Dead’ and Bret Harte’s Gabriel Conroy: The Na- ture of the Feast” (Yale Journal of Criticism) and “The Joyce of Eating in Ulysses: Feast, Famine, and the Humble Potato” (Hungry Words: Images of the Famine in the Irish Canon). 354 Critical Insights
